Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Definition of physiotherapy? Explain in detail the principles of evidence based practice in physiotherapy?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1a, 1d — Definition & scope; Principles of Evidence Based Practice

★ Memory hook — EBP = E′·E′·P′ — Evidence + Expertise + Patient values (three legs of one stool). The five steps are the five A’s in order: Ask → Acquire → Appraise → Apply → Assess.

1Introduction

Physiotherapy (World Physiotherapy, the body renamed from WCPT in 2019) is the service provided by physiotherapists to individuals and populations to develop, maintain and restore maximum movement and functional ability throughout the lifespan — including where movement and function are threatened by ageing, injury, disease, disorder or environmental factors. Three words carry the whole definition: movement, function and lifespan. It is a primary-contact, autonomous profession that works within the WHO ICF biopsychosocial framework — it treats not the disease but the person's function and participation. (The APTA frames the same idea as “optimising movement to improve the human experience.”)

2Background and principles

EBP (Sackett) is the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of the current best research evidence, integrated with clinical expertise and the patient's values and circumstances, in decisions about the care of individual patients. Its three legs form one stool: best evidence, clinical expertise, patient values. Remove any one and practice is no longer evidence-based — evidence without expertise is cook-book therapy, expertise without evidence is opinion, and both without patient values are paternalism. The 5 A's — Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, Assess — are the operational principles, and the hierarchy of evidence is the yardstick by which acquired evidence is graded.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

  • Ask — turn the clinical problem into a focused, answerable PICO/PICOT question (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time).
  • Acquire — search systematically: PubMed/MEDLINE, PEDro (the physiotherapy-specific database), and the Cochrane Library, using MeSH terms and Boolean operators.
  • Appraise — judge validity, magnitude and applicability of each study, using the hierarchy of evidence and appraisal tools (the PEDro scale for RCTs; GRADE for certainty).
  • Apply — integrate the appraised evidence with your clinical expertise and the patient's preferences, culture and finances.
  • Assess (audit) — evaluate the patient outcome and your own performance; the result feeds the next cycle of the loop.

Hierarchy of evidence (strongest to weakest): systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs → individual RCTs → cohort studies → case–control studies → cross-sectional studies → case series and case reports → expert opinion and bench research. The level is a guide, not a verdict: a large, well-conducted cohort may outweigh a small, flawed RCT.

Step (5 A's)Physiotherapy illustration
Ask“In chronic low-back pain, is motor-control exercise better than general exercise for reducing disability at 3 months?”
AcquireSearch PEDro and PubMed for RCTs and systematic reviews
AppraiseCheck randomisation, blinding and PEDro score; note the effect size
ApplyBlend with the patient's goals, cost and beliefs (a daily-wage worker)
AssessRe-measure disability at 3 months and audit the decision
Fig 1 — the 5-step EBP cycle around the evidence-expertise-patient core. Reproduce this and the pyramid in any EBP answer.

4Answer

Stating the principles in order. (1) Physiotherapy is defined by movement and function across the lifespan and is practised autonomously within the ICF. (2) Evidence-based practice rests on the triad of best evidence + clinical expertise + patient values. (3) The evidence is found by the five A's — Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, Assess — and graded by the hierarchy of evidence. (4) Appraisal weighs internal validity, effect size and applicability, using tools such as the PEDro scale for RCTs and GRADE for certainty of evidence. (5) Application is patient-specific: the best-supported technique must still be affordable and acceptable — in Indian practice, whether a daily-wage patient can sustain shockwave therapy is itself part of the evidence-based decision.

Conclusion. Physiotherapy is the autonomous, movement-focused health profession defined by World Physiotherapy; its practice is kept current, accountable and patient-centred by evidence-based practice, which is not a hierarchy to memorise but a five-step decision loop wrapped around the evidence–expertise–patient triad.

Students write a lovely definition and stop — the five steps with a physiotherapy example are what carry 5 of the 10 marks. Naming PEDro as the physiotherapy-specific database earns a bonus smile.

5Recent advances

  • Hoffmann et al. (2021) — masterclass establishing shared decision making as the final step of evidence-based practice and a core competency in physical therapy, linking research evidence to patient-centred care.
  • Fujimoto et al. (2022) — multicentre randomised controlled trial showing that teaching clinical practice guidelines together with shared decision making raises therapists' EBP self-efficacy more than either approach taught alone.
  • Grenfell & Soundy (2022) — systematic review and thematic synthesis in musculoskeletal physiotherapy showing most patients want to be involved, with mutual trust and two-way communication the enabling conditions.
  • Maher et al. (2003) — reliability study of the 11-item PEDro scale, which became the standard physiotherapy-specific tool for appraising RCT quality and underpins the PEDro evidence database.
  • Fernández-Domínguez et al. (2017) — developed and psychometrically validated the Health-Sciences Evidence-Based Practice (HS-EBP) questionnaire, measuring the full EBP process from literature search to outcome evaluation in practising clinicians.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 1 (a, d).
  2. Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM. Churchill Livingstone (syllabus Paper-I reference 5).
  3. Herbert R, Jamtvedt G, Hagen K, Mead J. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy. Churchill Livingstone (syllabus Paper-I reference 6).
  4. World Physiotherapy policy statement — description of physiotherapy.
  5. Pacheco-Brousseau L, Stacey D, Ben Amor S, Poitras S. Shared decision-making conceptual models for physiotherapy: a theory analysis. Physiotherapy. 2022;115:1–9.
  6. People’s Experience of Shared Decision Making in Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy: A Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis. Behav Sci. 2022;12(1):12.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Write the ethical issues faced in clinical practice of physiotherapy?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 2 — Core Professional Values; ethical issues in practice; ICMR guidelines

★ Memory hook — Ethics runs on A-B-N-J: Autonomy, Beneficence, Non-maleficence, Justice — “All Beneficial care, Never unjust.” Then list the Indian issues: consent, confidentiality, scope, overtreatment, boundaries, documentation, equity, advertising.

1Introduction

Beauchamp & Childress's four principles anchor clinical ethics: autonomy (respect the patient's informed choices), beneficence (act in the patient's best interest), non-maleficence (do no harm) and justice (fair, equitable distribution of services). The profession adds two normative documents: the World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice and, in India, the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines.

Fig 2 — The four-principles quadrant with patient welfare at the centre. Two minutes to draw, instantly shows the examiner you know the ethical scaffolding before you list the issues.

2Background and principles

Physiotherapy is a primary-contact, autonomous profession: the therapist is often the first — and only — decision-maker for the patient. That autonomy, combined with the knowledge imbalance between clinician and patient and the intimate, hands-on nature of treatment, is why ethical issues surface daily in an Indian OPD. Ethics is not a separate subject but the scaffolding on which every clinical decision rests; the four principles tell us what to weigh, and the codes and guidelines tell us how to behave.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

  • Consent and autonomy — treating without adequate explanation; in India, families often decide for the patient, so negotiating informed consent across language and literacy barriers is a daily issue.
  • Confidentiality — sensitive conditions (HIV status, occupational-injury claims) discussed in open treatment areas or with employers without consent.
  • Scope of practice and referral — treating beyond competence (e.g. manipulating the cervical spine without training) or handling red-flag cases that needed medical referral.
  • Overtreatment and commercial pressure — unnecessarily prolonged packages; outcome-driven billing exploits the knowledge imbalance.
  • Dual relationships and boundaries — treating relatives or close acquaintances, gifts, or social-media friendships that cloud clinical judgement.
  • Documentation and record keeping — poor notes that fail medicolegal scrutiny; tele-rehabilitation consent and data privacy.
  • Equity — refusing treatment to patients with infectious disease; gender-related discomfort (female patients with male therapists in India and vice versa); access for the poor.
  • Advertising and misrepresentation — promising cures (“guaranteed back-pain relief”) violates honesty.

The ICMR 2017 guidelines and RIPE 2020 add institutional ethics-committee approval, voluntary participation and compensation for trial injury — directly relevant to any postgraduate dissertation involving patients.

4Answer

How to resolve them. Ethical practice is institutionalised, not improvised: an active institutional ethics committee, adherence to the World Physiotherapy Standards and the IAP code, continuing education, peer review, honest documentation and transparent billing. Where a conflict is genuine — an employer demanding a package the patient does not need — the physiotherapist's duty is to the patient, documented and, if necessary, escalated to the ethics committee.

Conclusion. The primary-contact autonomy that gives physiotherapy its strength also makes these safeguards essential. The profession's social contract rests on placing patient welfare at the centre of every decision — consent, confidentiality, competence, honesty and equity are not optional courtesies but the ethical minimum of practice.

Marks come from explaining issues with an Indian clinical example each — not listing single words. An answer without the four principles and without ICMR mention rarely crosses 6.

5Recent advances

  • World Health Organization (2021) — its guidance on the ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health stresses human oversight, transparency, fairness/justice and accountability shared between developers, clinicians and institutions.
  • Hinteregger et al. (2024) — scoping review of the ethical dimensions of digital technology-assisted physiotherapy, underpinning an ethics-education toolkit for physiotherapists covering data privacy, remote consent and equity of access.
  • Veras et al. (2025) — rapid review of the ethical and equity dimensions of telerehabilitation in physiotherapy and occupational therapy, finding inconsistent reporting of patient autonomy, privacy, adverse events and access disparities.
  • Karaibrahimoglu et al. (2024) — scoping review mapping the ethical issues of telehealth and artificial intelligence in work-related musculoskeletal disorders — bias, transparency, data privacy and accountability for errors.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 2 (a–d).
  2. ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research involving Human Participants, 2017 (syllabus Paper-I reference 9).
  3. World Physiotherapy (2011) Standards of Physical Therapy Practice (reference 8).
  4. Beauchamp TL, Childress JF. Principles of Biomedical Ethics. (standard ethics reference)
  5. Gorman-Badar D, Ditwiler RE. AI Ethics: Unveiling and Shaping AI Technologies. APTA Magazine. 2024 (August).
  6. Ethical considerations in telehealth and artificial intelligence for work-related musculoskeletal disorders: a scoping review. Work. 2024.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Importance of pilot study in clinical research?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3a — Conceiving the research question & developing the study plan

★ Memory hook — Pilot study: tests the process, never the hypothesis — “P for Process, not Proof”.

1Introduction

A pilot study is a small-scale, preliminary run of a planned study, performed on a limited number of participants — usually about 10% of the intended sample, or a fixed 10–30 subjects — to test whether the full study can be carried out as designed. Its purpose is feasibility, not proof: it answers the question "can this trial be done?" and never "does this treatment work?". In an RGUHS MPT dissertation, where the student has a single OPD, one supervisor and a two-year window, the pilot is the most cost-effective safeguard against a study that collapses halfway for reasons that were entirely predictable. It examines the process — recruitment, consent, intervention delivery, instruments, data capture and cost — and its findings are reported as feasibility outcomes, never as trial results.

2Background and principles

The pilot stands at the start of the research pipeline, between the written protocol and the definitive trial, and its guiding principle is that a study should be rehearsed before it is performed. Six purposes recur in every textbook and on every examiner's mark sheet:

  1. Feasibility of recruitment and retention: can the planned number of eligible patients actually be enrolled in the available time, and will they remain in the study? The pilot reports a recruitment rate per month and a drop-out rate, from which the main trial's timeline and target are recalculated.
  2. Protocol and intervention refinement: does the intervention work in practice — the exercise dosage, session length, number of visits and timing of outcome measurement? Impractical procedures surface here, for example a 90-minute assessment that no working patient completes.
  3. Instrument testing: are the outcome measures understood and completed correctly? Missing-item rates, floor and ceiling effects, and the readability of a translated tool (does the Kannada SPADI read naturally to a rural patient?) are legitimate pilot outcomes.
  4. Sample-size estimation: the pilot supplies an observed mean and standard deviation, or an event rate, that replaces the researcher's guesswork in the power calculation for the main trial.
  5. Resources, cost and data management: staff time, consumables, equipment, budget, and whether the case-record form or electronic data-capture sheet captures the variables cleanly.
  6. Safety and acceptability: early evidence on adverse events, tolerability and patient burden — the information an ethics committee needs before approving a larger exposure.

Two terms should be separated: a pilot study asks a specific feasibility question about a planned trial, whereas a feasibility study is the wider family of small studies that estimate whether a future trial is worth doing. An internal pilot is embedded within the main trial; an external pilot stands alone and its data are never pooled with the main analysis.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

Use — a worked Indian example. Before a randomised trial of eccentric versus concentric quadriceps training in patellofemoral pain, a pilot of 8 patients revealed two problems: the daily visual-analogue pain diary confused participants (a high missing-item rate), and two patients dropped out because of travel cost. The main trial therefore switched to a numeric pain-rating scale recorded at weekly visits and offered transport reimbursement — two changes that would otherwise have wrecked the larger study.

Limitations. A small sample cannot confirm or refute the main hypothesis: estimates are unstable, and a promising pilot result may still fail in the definitive trial. Pilot data must never be pooled into the main analysis (that inflates the type I error), and pilot results are interpreted only as feasibility outcomes. The commonest student error is to treat the pilot as a mini-trial and quote a p-value from it.

Question the pilot answersDecision it informs in the main trial
Recruitment rate per monthFeasible sample size and timeline
Drop-out rateInflation of the sample-size target
Observed SD of the outcomePower calculation
Missing-item and ceiling effectsChoice of outcome measure
Cost and staff timeBudget and funding application

4Answer

How to run a pilot, step by step. (1) State the feasibility objectives and pre-specify progression criteria before data collection — for example, recruit at least 80% of the target within the pilot window, retain at least 85%, and complete at least 90% of outcome measures. (2) Obtain ethics-committee approval; a pilot is still research on human participants. (3) Recruit the small sample using exactly the inclusion criteria of the main trial. (4) Deliver the intervention and measurement precisely as the main trial will. (5) Analyse feasibility endpoints — rates, proportions and SDs — not treatment effects. (6) Report transparently using the CONSORT extension for pilot and feasibility trials, and decide against the progression criteria whether to proceed, modify or abandon the main trial.

Conclusion. A pilot study is the dress rehearsal for the main trial: it tests the research process — recruitment, protocol, instruments, sample-size variance, cost and data management — and never the hypothesis. Its findings are reported as feasibility outcomes, its data are never pooled into the definitive analysis, and its progression criteria decide whether the larger study goes ahead. Skipping it does not save time; it only postpones the discovery of a fatal flaw until it can no longer be fixed.

5Recent advances

  • Eldridge et al. (2016) — the CONSORT 2010 extension to randomised pilot and feasibility trials, a 26-item checklist that standardises how feasibility studies are reported and interpreted.
  • Thabane et al. (2010) — widely cited tutorial defining feasibility objectives, success criteria and CONSORT-style reporting for pilot studies, now a standard reference for physiotherapy trial protocols.
  • Mellor et al. (2023) — recommendations for prespecified progression criteria (often red-amber-green) for deciding whether to proceed from an external pilot to the definitive trial.
  • Bond et al. (2023) — updated the conceptual framework for pilot and feasibility studies to include internal pilot studies, with their ethical, funding and policy implications.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3a (iii–vi).
  2. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins (syllabus Paper-I reference 11).
  3. Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics. 4th ed. CRC Press (reference 12).
  4. Eldridge SM, Chan CL, Campbell MJ, et al. CONSORT 2010 statement: extension to randomised pilot and feasibility trials. BMJ. 2016;355:i5239.
  5. Mellor K, Albury C, Dutton SJ, Eldridge S, Hopewell S. Recommendations for progression criteria during external randomised pilot trial design, conduct, analysis and reporting. Pilot Feasibility Stud. 2023;9:59.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. How would you differentiate between simple random sampling and complex random sampling designs? Explain clearly by giving examples?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3a-iv — Choosing study subjects: specification, sampling and recruitment

★ Memory hook — Sampling ladder: Systematic = every k-th from a list; Stratified = strata first, random inside each; Cluster = whole groups at random.

1Introduction

Sampling is the process of selecting a subset of a population so that conclusions drawn from the sample can be generalised to the population with known confidence. The organising distinction is between simple random sampling — the pure, unrestricted probability method — and complex (restricted) random sampling, the family of designs (stratified, cluster, systematic and multi-stage) that add a structure to the selection in order to gain precision or to save money and logistics. Every member of the sampling frame has a known, non-zero chance of selection under both, but they differ in how that chance is arranged, in the frame they require, and in the precision and cost they deliver. The examiner wants the differences stated feature by feature, each illustrated with a number.

2Background and principles

Simple random sampling (SRS). Every member of the sampling frame has an equal and independent chance of selection. It is performed by lottery, random-number tables or computer-generated random numbers. Example: drawing 60 of the 400 registered low-back-pain patients on a hospital list using random numbers. SRS is the theoretical gold standard — unbiased and assumption-free — but it demands a complete sampling frame, and when the population is geographically dispersed the sample is spread thinly, making data collection expensive.

Complex (restricted) random sampling. These designs restrict or structure the randomisation to overcome one of the weaknesses of SRS. Stratified sampling first divides the population into homogeneous strata (sex, disease severity, age band) and then takes a simple random sample within each stratum, often proportionally; it guarantees representation of small subgroups and improves precision. Cluster sampling randomly selects natural groups — schools, villages, wards — and studies everyone inside the chosen clusters; it is the cheapest method for dispersed populations but less precise, because members of a cluster resemble one another (intra-cluster correlation). Systematic sampling takes every k-th person from a list after a random start (k = frame size ÷ sample size); it is quick and list-based but risks periodicity. Multi-stage sampling combines these in successive stages (state → district → hospital → patient) for large community surveys.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

Each complex design is a trade-off. Stratified sampling buys precision and guaranteed subgroup coverage at the cost of needing a list of the strata; cluster and multi-stage sampling buy economy at the cost of precision (the design effect); systematic sampling buys speed at the risk of a periodic list. All of them remain probability designs — the key teaching point is that stratified sampling is not quota sampling, because within each stratum the selection is still random. The designs side by side:

FeatureSimple random samplingComplex random sampling
Selection ruleEqual, independent chance for every memberRandom selection within a fixed structure
Frame neededComplete list of all membersList of strata or clusters only
PrecisionBaselineStratified ↑; cluster ↓
Subgroup representationChance-dependentStratified guarantees it
Cost / logisticsHigh for dispersed populationsCluster and multi-stage cheapest

4Answer

The differentiation, stated plainly. SRS selects individuals directly and independently from the whole frame; complex designs first impose a structure — strata, clusters, a list order or successive stages — and then randomise within it. SRS is simple and unbiased but frame-hungry and costly for scattered populations. Stratified sampling sharpens precision and protects small subgroups (a TKR study sampling male and female patients separately in a 1:2 ratio because the clinic population is one-third women). Cluster sampling cuts cost for wide community surveys (randomly picking 6 of Bengaluru's 40 physiotherapy colleges and surveying every final-year student in them). Systematic sampling offers a fast list-based alternative (every 5th OPD patient from a random Monday start). Multi-stage sampling makes large surveys feasible (Karnataka → 4 districts → 2 PHCs each → all adults screened for knee OA).

Choosing between them. Use SRS when a complete frame exists and the population is compact; move to a complex design when the frame is incomplete, when a small subgroup must be represented (stratified), or when the population is dispersed and travel cost dominates (cluster and multi-stage). Always report the design, the frame and the achieved sample.

Conclusion. Simple random sampling is the theoretical reference standard — equal, independent selection — but it needs a complete frame and is costly across wide geographies. Complex random designs trade a little simplicity for precision (stratified) or logistics (cluster, multi-stage, systematic), and the choice is driven by the population's structure, the available frame and the study's budget. The differentiating marks lie in the examples with numbers — "every 5th patient", "6 of 40 colleges" — and in stating that stratified samples are still random within strata.

5Recent advances

  • Thompson (1990) — introduced adaptive cluster sampling, in which selection is tailored during data collection so effort concentrates where high values cluster, improving efficiency for rare or spatially clustered traits such as disease prevalence.
  • Groves & Heeringa (2006) — introduced responsive survey designs that use paradata and targeted recruitment across data-collection phases to reduce nonresponse bias and control costs.
  • Mecatti et al. (2023) — proposed sequential adaptive (Poisson-based) designs that update selection probabilities as data accumulate, improving design efficiency for a rare trait unevenly spread over an area, as in national tuberculosis prevalence surveys.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3a-iv.
  2. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. (reference 11).
  3. Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics. 4th ed. (reference 12).
  4. Panahbehagh B, Tillé Y, Khanzadi A. Sampling with adaptive drawing probabilities. Survey Methodology. 2023;49(1).
  5. Sequential adaptive strategies for sampling rare clustered populations. Statistical Methods & Applications. 2023.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Write in detail the fundamentals of qualitative research methods?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3b-vi, 3c-iv — Fundamentals of qualitative research; designing qualitative studies

★ Memory hook — Qualitative = words, not numbers. Designs P-G-E-N (Phenomenology, Grounded theory, Ethnography, Narrative); rigour C-T-D-C (Credibility, Transferability, Dependability, Confirmability).

1Introduction

Qualitative research explores meanings, experiences and processes — the "why" and "how" — rather than measuring quantities ("how much"). It answers questions an RCT cannot: how do stroke survivors in rural Karnataka experience self-management, why do patients abandon their home programme, or how do therapists actually make clinical decisions? The data are words, images and observations, and the researcher is the instrument. Its value in physiotherapy lies precisely here: it explains the mechanisms of adherence, communication and lived disability that quantitative measures capture only as numbers.

2Background and principles

Qualitative research rests on a different paradigm — interpretivist rather than positivist — in which reality is socially constructed and the goal is understanding, not statistical generalisation. Four major designs cover most work, remembered as P-G-E-N:

  • Phenomenology — describes the lived experience of a phenomenon (patients' experience of chronic low-back pain).
  • Grounded theory — builds a theory from the data through constant comparison, to explain a process (how adherence to a home programme develops).
  • Ethnography — studies the culture of a group (pain beliefs within a community).
  • Narrative inquiry / case study — follows the story of illness over time.

The choice of design follows the question: experience → phenomenology; process → grounded theory; culture → ethnography; individual story → narrative.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

Sampling and data collection. Sampling is purposive — information-rich cases are chosen deliberately — and is extended by snowball recruitment for hidden populations. Enrolment continues until data saturation, when no new themes emerge (often after 10–15 in-depth interviews). Tools include semi-structured in-depth interviews, focus-group discussions, non-participant observation and document review, with audio-recording by consent and verbatim transcription.

Analysis. Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke: familiarisation → coding → generating themes → reviewing → defining → reporting) or content analysis; the framework approach for policy research; software (NVivo, ATLAS.ti) assists but never replaces the analyst. Analysis proceeds simultaneously with data collection.

Rigour and limitations. A qualitative study is judged by trustworthiness, not sample size, using Lincoln & Guba's four criteria: credibility (triangulation, member-checking), transferability (thick description), dependability (audit trail) and confirmability (reflexivity). Its limitation is that findings are not statistically generalisable; its strength is depth, context and the patient's voice.

4Answer

How a qualitative study is conducted, step by step. (1) Frame an open, exploratory question. (2) Choose the design from P-G-E-N. (3) Select participants purposively and continue to saturation. (4) Collect data by interview, focus group or observation, recording and transcribing verbatim. (5) Analyse thematically, coding and comparing until themes stabilise. (6) Establish trustworthiness through triangulation, member-checking, an audit trail and reflexivity. (7) Report with thick description so the reader can judge transferability.

One viva trap. Qualitative research is not "research without numbers because it is easier" — it is a deliberate paradigm with its own rigour. In Indian physiotherapy, mixed-methods designs are increasingly used: an interview to explore beliefs alongside a goniometer to measure range.

Conclusion. The fundamentals of qualitative research are its paradigm (interpretivist), its designs (P-G-E-N), its purposive sampling to saturation, its interview/focus-group/observation tools, its thematic analysis, and its Lincoln & Guba criteria of trustworthiness. In physiotherapy it answers the questions numbers cannot — how patients experience pain, why adherence succeeds or fails, and how practice itself is shaped — and, used beside quantitative evidence, it gives a fuller picture of the patient's world.

5Recent advances

  • Braun & Clarke (2024) — reflexive thematic analysis is now the dominant qualitative method; their Reflexive Thematic Analysis Reporting Guidelines (RTARG) replace checklist-based reporting such as COREQ.
  • Malterud et al. (2016) — introduced "information power" as a model for sample size in qualitative interview studies, now widely used to justify sample adequacy in physiotherapy qualitative research.
  • Kalu et al. (2022) — systematic mapping review of 20 years of physiotherapy qualitative research found variable, mostly low reporting quality, with reflexivity and member-checking often missing.
  • Barradell (2022) — qualitative portraits of 'learning to be a physiotherapist' exemplify how qualitative studies examine the process of developing clinical competency and the patient-therapist relationship.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3b-vi and 3c-iv.
  2. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. (reference 11).
  3. Braun V, Clarke V. Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qual Res Psychol. 2006;3:77–101. (primary method reference)
  4. Braun V, Clarke V. One size fits all? What counts as quality practice in (reflexive) thematic analysis? Qual Res Psychol. 2021;18(3):328–352.
  5. Kalu ME, Okoh AC, Okeke C, et al. Qualitative research in physiotherapy: a systematic mapping review of 20 years of literature from sub-Saharan Africa. BMC Med Res Methodol. 2021.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write note on fundamentals of Human energy transfer?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4a — Fundamentals of Human Energy Transfer

★ Memory hook — Energy systems run 10 : 2 : ∞ — ATP–PC about 10 seconds, glycolysis about 2 minutes, oxidative forever.

1Introduction

The first law (conservation of energy): energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted — the human machine converts the chemical energy of food into mechanical work, heat and stored energy. The second law: conversions are inefficient, so much is lost as heat — which is why exercising bodies warm up. Biogenic molecules are reduced (energy-rich) and are oxidised to CO2 and H2O to release free energy.

2Physiology

Cells cannot use food energy directly; all transfers pass through ATP, whose terminal phosphate bond releases about 7.3 kcal/mol on hydrolysis. ATP is regenerated by phosphorylation of ADP through coupled reactions: substrate-level (glycolysis, creatine phosphate) and oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondrial electron-transport chain. The creatine-phosphate (CP) shuttle provides the fastest regeneration: ADP + CP → ATP + creatine, catalysed by creatine kinase. Three systems share the load:

  • ATP–PC (phosphagen) — immediate, about 10 s of explosive power, anaerobic, no lactate.
  • Anaerobic glycolysis — 10 s to about 2 min of high-intensity effort; rapid ATP but limited by H+/lactate accumulation.
  • Oxidative (aerobic) system — carbohydrate and fat oxidation; unlimited duration at lower intensity, dominant after about 2 min; fat yields more ATP per gram but needs more oxygen.

3Pathophysiology

When energy supply cannot keep pace with demand, or the machinery of oxidative metabolism is impaired, performance falls and fatigue sets in. Whole-body mechanical efficiency is only about 20–25% (cycle ergometry); the rest is heat — the physiological basis of warm-up, of thermoregulation during exercise, and of caloric-expenditure calculations (1 L O2 ≈ 5 kcal; 1 MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min). Training shifts substrate use (fat oxidation at higher intensities in the trained) and raises the lactate threshold — the underpinning of every endurance prescription. Clinically, the oxygen deficit at the onset of exercise, and the excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) that repays it, explain why interval training and adequate recovery shape the metabolic stimulus.

4Answer

Fig 6 — The power–duration curve with the three energy systems fenced off along the time axis. One curve, three systems, full marks for Q6.

Fick's equation governs the aerobic ceiling: VO2 = cardiac output × arteriovenous oxygen difference (VO2 = Q × (a–v)O2). The heart can deliver only as much oxygen as the muscles can extract; training raises both sides of the equation, which is why the aerobic system improves with endurance work.

Matching system to physiotherapy activity. The phosphagen system powers a single maximal effort — a hoist-assisted transfer or one maximal lift; glycolysis powers repeated 30-second efforts such as a stair-climb or a short burst of high-intensity gait training; the oxidative system underpins a 6-minute walk test, a long walking programme or cardiac rehabilitation. The ~20–25% mechanical efficiency explains exercise-induced heat and the need for hydration, and caloric-expenditure estimates (1 L O2 ≈ 5 kcal) underpin every endurance and weight-management prescription.

Conclusion. Human energy transfer is the conversion of food energy into ATP through three integrated systems — phosphagen, glycolytic and oxidative — whose relative contribution is set by exercise intensity and duration. Matching the system to the task is the essence of exercise prescription.

This is a physiology-of-exercise question in a research-paper wrapper — connect each system to a physiotherapy activity (phosphagen = a single hoist transfer in the gym; glycolytic = 2-min TUG repetitions; oxidative = a walking programme). Fick's equation can cameo for the aerobic system.

5Recent advances

  • Brooks (1986) — proposed the lactate shuttle, showing lactate is a major oxidative fuel and signalling molecule shuttled between tissues rather than merely a metabolic waste product; the foundation of modern exercise-metabolism thinking.
  • Zhang et al. (2019) — discovered histone lactylation, establishing lactate as a signalling molecule that links exercise metabolism to gene expression and substrate partitioning.
  • Hargreaves & Spriet (2020) — authoritative review of skeletal muscle energy metabolism during exercise, quantifying how phosphocreatine, glycogenolysis and oxidative phosphorylation interact as intensity and duration change — the basis for energy-system targeting in exercise prescription.
  • Smith et al. (2023) — Nature Reviews synthesis of exercise metabolism and adaptation showing how acute exercise and training remodel mitochondrial and metabolic networks, providing the mechanistic rationale for exercise as therapy.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 4a, 4g.
  2. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance. 8th ed. Lippincott (syllabus Paper-I reference 13).
  3. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier.
  4. Brooks GA. The Science and Translation of Lactate Shuttle Theory. Cell Metab. 2018;27(4):757–785.
  5. Brooks GA, Arevalo JA, Osmond AD, et al. Tracing the lactate shuttle to the mitochondrial reticulum. Exp Mol Med. 2022;54:1332–1347.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Briefly prescribe the exercise protocol for weight control?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4f — Body composition, evaluation, obesity and weight control

★ Memory hook — Weight control numbers: deficit 500–750 kcal/day → 0.5–1 kg/week; goal 5–10% body weight in 3–6 months. FITT = Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

1Introduction

Weight control means achieving and maintaining a healthy body composition by balancing energy intake against energy expenditure. The clinical aim is not cosmetic weight loss but the reduction of the metabolic and mechanical consequences of excess adiposity: a 5–10% loss over 3–6 months already improves glycaemia, blood pressure and knee-joint load. For an Indian patient the thresholds arrive early — obesity is defined at BMI ≥ 25 kg/m² (overweight 23–24.9), not the Western 30 — and central obesity at a waist of ≥ 90 cm in men and ≥ 80 cm in women (Misra, JAPI 2009). Baseline assessment before prescribing: BMI and waist circumference, body composition if available, resting blood pressure and blood sugar, joint status (the knees take the first load), PAR-Q+ screening, and current medication.

2Physiology

Weight falls only in negative energy balance. Total energy expenditure has three components: the resting metabolic rate (about 60–70% of daily expenditure, and the largest lever), the thermic effect of food (about 10%), and physical activity (20–30%, and the only component we can prescribe directly). The practical arithmetic is a daily deficit of 500–750 kcal, which yields about 0.5–1 kg of loss per week — roughly a 1200–1500 kcal diet for women and 1500–1800 for men, plus exercise. Exercise itself contributes only 200–400 kcal per session, so diet and activity must act together; this is why exercise alone rarely outpaces a calorie surplus.

Activity is quantified in METs (metabolic equivalents; 1 MET = 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min): brisk walking is about 4 METs and cycling about 8, so a 30-minute walk for a 70 kg patient costs roughly 130–150 kcal — the energy of about one chapati. Two further physiological levers matter. Resistance training preserves lean mass during energy restriction (which would otherwise fall, lowering resting metabolic rate and making relapse likely), and each kilogram of muscle gained raises resting expenditure. Exercise also improves insulin sensitivity and cardiorespiratory fitness even when the scale barely moves, and a single session raises post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), a small but real additional cost.

3Pathophysiology

Obesity is a chronic, relapsing disease in which excess adiposity drives dysfunction across systems: increased mechanical load on the weight-bearing joints (knees and lumbar spine first), insulin resistance and type-2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, and reduced cardiorespiratory fitness. Adipose tissue is also metabolically active, secreting adipokines and inflammatory cytokines that sustain low-grade inflammation and atherogenesis. In the Indian phenotype ("thin-fat"), abdominal (central) obesity and metabolic syndrome appear at a lower BMI than in Western populations, which is precisely why waist circumference is used alongside BMI to define risk. Before prescribing, review the comorbidities that modify the programme: hypoglycaemia risk in diabetics on insulin or sulfonylureas (advise carrying glucose and coordinating the dose with the physician), uncontrolled hypertension (defer if BP ≥ 180/110 until controlled), and painful knees or low back from the mechanical load.

4Answer

The prescription, by FITT.

PrinciplePrescription
FrequencyAerobic 5–7 days/week; resistance 2–3 non-consecutive days/week
IntensityModerate — 40–60% heart-rate reserve, or RPE 11–13 (Borg 6–20), talk-test pace
Time150 min/week building to 250–300 min; 30–60 min/day, accumulated in ≥ 10-min bouts
TypeLoad-friendly aerobic first — brisk walking, cycling, swimming/aqua-jogging; plus large-muscle resistance (8–10 exercises, 2–3 sets of 10–15 at 60–70% 1RM)

Progression and precautions. Progress volume before intensity — add roughly 5–10 minutes of tolerated walking per fortnight before touching speed or incline. Protect joints: aquatic exercise, cycles and graded walking paths for the painful knee; cushioned footwear; avoid deep squats early. In the Indian climate, schedule outdoor sessions for early morning or evening and enforce hydration. Watch for knee/back pain (modify mode), exercise-induced bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia in medicated diabetics and heat intolerance.

Behaviour and maintenance. Adherence is the real prescription: written goals, step counters (build to 8,000–10,000 steps/day), exercise logs, walking groups and family involvement — in Indian households the kitchen decides the calorie side of the equation, so involve whoever cooks. Reassess monthly with waist circumference and walk time, not the scale alone. Maintenance needs 200–300 min/week of activity with periodic weigh-ins, because relapse prevention is the true challenge.

Conclusion. The protocol for weight control is a 500–750 kcal/day deficit plus 150–300 minutes weekly of moderate aerobic exercise, resistance training twice or thrice weekly to preserve lean mass, and behavioural scaffolding, all progressed gradually and monitored by waist circumference and function rather than weight alone. In the Indian context, where central obesity is common and activity low, the prescription must be realistic, affordable and built around brisk walking, cycling and home-based resistance work.

5Recent advances

  • Rubino et al. (2025) — the Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission redefines clinical obesity using functional criteria rather than BMI alone, confirming excess adiposity with waist or body-fat measures.
  • Jakicic et al. (2024) — the ACSM consensus statement reaffirms at least 150 min/week of moderate activity, progressing to 200-300 min/week for weight-loss maintenance, with no single mode shown superior.
  • Bull et al. (2020) — the WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour, the first global guidelines to give specific recommendations on sedentary time and for people living with chronic conditions or disability.
  • Bellicha et al. (2021) — EASO overview of 12 systematic reviews (149 studies) showing exercise produces modest weight and fat loss and visceral fat loss, that resistance training best preserves lean mass during weight loss, and that HIIT equals moderate-intensity training at matched energy expenditure.
  • Locatelli et al. (2024) — review arguing that tailored resistance training should be added to GLP-1-based pharmacotherapy to preserve muscle mass, strength and function during weight loss.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 4f.
  2. ACSM. Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription / Resource Manual (MSK syllabus reference 12).
  3. McArdle, Katch & Katch. Exercise Physiology. 8th ed. (Paper-I reference 13).
  4. Misra A et al. JAPI 2009 consensus (Indian cutoffs).
  5. Physical Activity and Excess Body Weight and Adiposity for Adults: American College of Sports Medicine Consensus Statement. Transl J ACSM. 2024;9(4).
  6. Rubino F, Cummings DE, Eckel RH, et al. Definition and diagnostic criteria of clinical obesity. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2025;13(3):221–262.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Analyze the Instrumentation for neuromuscular electrical stimulation?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 5c — Instrumentation for NMES

★ Memory hook — Russian current: 2.5 kHz carrier, 50 bursts/s, 10:50 on:off. Motor NMES: 35–50 Hz, 200–400 µs, duty cycle 1:3–1:5.

1Introduction

NMES instrumentation: mains/power supply (battery → stabilised DC) → oscillator/pulse generator (sets frequency, pulse duration via timing circuits) → control/timer unit (on-off cycle, ramp) → amplifier (raises the signal to the required voltage/current) → output/transformer + coupling (safety isolation, charge-balanced output) → electrodes → tissue. Modern units are digital: microprocessor-generated pulsed currents with user-set parameters.

2Background and principles

  • Waveform: symmetrical/asymmetrical biphasic pulsed current is preferred (charge-balanced → no skin irritation under electrodes; monophasic pulsed (faradic-type) causes chemical polarisation).
  • Frequency (pulses/s): 30–50 pps for functional tetanic contraction (typical NMES 35–50 Hz; Russian current 2.5 kHz carrier modulated at 50 bursts/s for torque); low rates (2–10 Hz) for sensory/analgesic or muscle-pumping effects.
  • Pulse duration: 200–400 μs suits motor stimulation of large muscles (shorter for small muscles).
  • Amplitude (intensity): to strong but comfortable tetany, typically 20–100 mA depending on impedance.
  • Duty cycle / on:off: duty cycle 1:3 to 1:5 (e.g., 10 s on, 30–50 s off) to postpone fatigue — stimulated muscle fatigues faster than voluntary contraction.
  • Ramp-up: 1–2 s for comfort.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

Large motor electrode over the muscle's motor point, smaller/dispersive electrode at the distal tendon or the opposite side of the belly; size governs current density; low-impedance hydrogel pads; skin preparation and exact motor-point mapping determine efficiency.

Avoid pacemakers/implanted devices, pregnancy over uterus, active malignancy in the region, thrombosis, and broken skin. Uses: muscle strengthening/re-education after injury or surgery (e.g., post-TKR quadriceps), disuse atrophy, NMES-assisted gait, oedema pumping, and preserving muscle plasticity (unit 5d).

4Answer

Fig 8 — The NMES block diagram: five boxes, each labelled with the parameter that box controls. Examiners give the diagram mark for exactly this label-per-block discipline.

Clinical application and conclusion. Every parameter the instrumentation exposes maps onto a physiological fact: frequency sets whether the muscle tetanises (35–50 Hz) or merely pumps (2–10 Hz); pulse duration (200–400 µs) decides which motor fibres are recruited; the duty cycle (1:3–1:5) postpones the fatigue that stimulated muscle is prone to; and a charge-balanced biphasic output avoids the skin irritation of monophasic currents. Matching the machine’s settings to the clinical goal — strengthening, re-education, oedema pumping or gait assistance — is what separates effective NMES from indiscriminate stimulation.

The examiner wants the analogy with physiology: every parameter you name, tie it to a nerve-physiology fact (frequency→tetany; duration→motor fibre recruitment threshold). And "charge-balanced biphasic prevents skin irritation" is a distinction line.

5Recent advances

  • Flodin et al. (2023) — wearable NMES pants with integrated textile electrodes increased femoral venous peak velocity 2-3-fold with minimal discomfort, supporting venous thromboembolism prevention.
  • Merhi et al. (2023) — printed dry electrodes integrated into a compressive stocking could be worn for more than seven days without inflammation, offering a gel-free, reusable alternative to reduce skin irritation.
  • Matsubara et al. (2023) — mm-order two-dimensional electrode arrays automatically identify and stimulate the motor point, individualising electrode position and size to improve comfort and adherence.
  • Maffiuletti et al. (2018) — special communication showing that NMES effectiveness is governed by the evoked force (muscle tension) rather than externally set parameters, and recommending tension-controlled, algorithm-based dosing in clinical practice.
  • Song et al. (2024) — battery-free, body-coupled textile (BCES) socks harvest ambient and static electricity to activate muscle during everyday activity, improving exercise performance and reducing fatigue.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 5 (a–e).
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. — membrane/action potential chapters.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — electrical muscle stimulation sections.
  4. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (MSK syllabus reference 10).
  5. Wearable Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation on Quadriceps Muscle Can Increase Venous Flow. Ann Biomed Eng. 2023;51:2518–2528.
  6. Unlocking the potential of neuromuscular electrical stimulation: achieving physical activity benefits. Front Sports Act Living. 2024;6:1507402.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Psychometric Properties of SPADI

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1 — Use of standardized scales; psychometric properties and interpretation

★ Memory hook — SPADI = 5 + 8 = 13 items, 0–100, higher = worse; MCID ≈ 8–10, MDC95 ≈ 18. QuickDASH cuts it to 11 items.

1Introduction

The SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index, Roach et al. 1991) is a 13-item, self-report, region-specific measure of shoulder pathology: 5 pain items (pain at its worst, lying on the involved side, reaching up high, touching the back of the neck, pushing with the involved arm) and 8 disability items (daily self-care and lifting tasks such as washing hair, washing the back, dressing and carrying heavy objects). Each item is scored on an 11-point numerical rating scale (0–10); the total (out of 130) is expressed as a percentage from 0 (perfect shoulder) to 100 (worst imaginable), so higher scores mean worse function. Its psychometric properties — reliability, validity and responsiveness — decide whether the numbers it produces can be trusted in an individual patient or in a trial.

2Background and principles

Reliability is the consistency of measurement. Internal consistency — the degree to which the items measure one construct — is high for the SPADI: Cronbach's α has ranged from about 0.86 to 0.98 across subscales and total in validation studies, above the 0.70 floor though near the 0.95 ceiling where items begin to repeat each other. Test–retest reliability — stability over 1–2 weeks in stable patients — is likewise high, with intraclass correlation coefficients commonly between 0.84 and 0.94 for the total score (the original 1991 sample reported more modest values near 0.64). Measurement error must be quoted beside reliability: on the 0–100 scale the minimal detectable change (MDC₉₅) is about 18 points, so a repeated-measurement difference smaller than that is indistinguishable from noise. Reliability also has an inter-rater and a cross-cultural dimension, discussed below.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

Validity. Content/face validity: items were developed from patients' own reports (37 patients in the original study), ensuring they reflect the construct patients care about. Construct validity: factor analysis supports a two-factor (pain and disability) structure, though some studies find a single dominant factor; convergent correlations with the DASH are moderate to strong (r ≈ 0.6–0.8), and correlations with goniometric ROM and pain ratings run in the expected direction. Criterion validity is the soft spot — there is no universally accepted gold standard for shoulder disability, so the SPADI anchors itself against ROM and clinical change. Cross-cultural validity: validated translations exist (Hindi, Kannada, Marathi, Tamil, Chinese, Portuguese), with equivalent factor structure.

Responsiveness and interpretation. Responsiveness — the ability to detect real change — is good across conditions from adhesive capsulitis to rotator-cuff pathology and post-arthroplasty follow-up, with effect sizes of 0.8–1.4. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID), the smallest change a patient would notice, is about 8–10 points (8, 10 and about 13 have all been reported), with values near the higher end after procedures such as arthroplasty. There are no floor or ceiling problems in typical MSK shoulder populations, unlike generic measures.

PropertyTypical valueMeaning
Internal consistencyCronbach's α 0.86–0.98Items measure one construct
Test–retest reliabilityICC 0.84–0.94Stable over 1–2 weeks
Measurement errorMDC₉₅ ≈ 18 pointsChange below this is noise
ResponsivenessEffect size 0.8–1.4Detects real change
Clinical importanceMCID ≈ 8–10 pointsChange the patient feels

4Answer

Using the SPADI. It is used to track an individual patient's progress and as a research endpoint, and it is free and takes only two to three minutes — an advantage in a busy Indian OPD. Read the numbers together: statistical significance decides whether a treatment beat noise; crossing the MCID decides whether the patient cares; and a change below the MDC cannot be claimed as change at all. Pair it with objective measures (ROM, strength) for a complete ICF picture, remembering that the SPADI maps largely to activity and participation rather than body structure. Validated Indian versions support its use across languages — the Hindi SPADI (internal consistency about 0.75 in overhead athletes, test–retest ICC about 0.87, MDC₉₅ about 14) and a Tamil version validated in the Hong Kong Physiotherapy Journal.

Conclusion. The psychometric profile of the SPADI — internal consistency α 0.86–0.98, test–retest ICC 0.84–0.94, MDC₉₅ ≈ 18, effect sizes 0.8–1.4 and an MCID of about 8–10 points — makes it a short, reliable, valid and responsive shoulder-specific measure suitable both for individual monitoring and for research. Its numbers are interpretable only through these properties: the same 9-point improvement can be noise in one context and a patient-felt success in another.

5Recent advances

  • KC et al. (2021) — COSMIN-based systematic review of translated SPADI versions that standardised the evaluation of its measurement properties across languages and populations.
  • Jerosch-Herold et al. (2018) — Rasch analysis concluded the SPADI should be treated as two separate subscales (pain and disability), the disability subscale not meeting strict interval-level criteria.
  • Furtado et al. (2019) — systematic review of cross-cultural adaptations finding most translations followed proper procedures but that psychometric testing of the adapted SPADI was often incomplete.
  • Ho et al. (2022) — the Malay SPADI (M-SPADI) established construct validity, internal consistency and test-retest reliability in patients with shoulder pain.
  • Porollan et al. (2024) — cross-cultural adaptation and validation of the Argentine SPADI confirmed reliability (ICC about 0.89) with a minimal detectable change about 6 and MCID about 18 points.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 1 (standardized scales & psychometric properties).
  2. Roach KE, Budiman-Mak E, Songsiridej N, Lertratanakul Y. Development of a shoulder pain and disability index. Arthritis Care Res. 1991;4:143–9. (primary)
  3. Williams JW et al. Responsive and important: SPADI vs SF-36. J Clin Epidemiol. (responsiveness evidence)
  4. Hicks CM. Research Methods for Clinical Therapists. (psychometric interpretation — Indian MPT standard)
  5. Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric properties of the Argentine version of the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI). JSES Int. 2024.
  6. Venturin D, Giannotta G, Pellicciari L, et al. Reliability and validity of the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index in a sample of patients with frozen shoulder. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2023;24:1–9.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. What is formulated intended learning outcomes? Explain in detail the six objectives of Bloom's Taxonomy?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 6c — Formulating ILOs; Tyler's principles, Bloom's Taxonomy, Miller's Pyramid

★ Memory hook — Bloom’s verbs climb R-U-A-A-E-C: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. Miller’s pyramid peaks at Does.

1Introduction

An Intended Learning Outcome (ILO) is a statement, written before teaching begins, of what the learner is expected to know, do or value at the end of a defined learning episode — the destination the teacher designs towards (Tyler's rationale: objectives → experiences → organisation → evaluation). Good ILOs are SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) and use observable action verbs ("demonstrate", "differentiate") rather than vague ones ("understand", "know"). The standard structure is: "By the end of this session, the student will be able to <action verb> <content> <context/standard>." Bloom's Taxonomy supplies the vocabulary of those action verbs, and the question asks for its six objectives in detail.

2Background and principles

ILOs are the anchor of constructive alignment (Biggs): teaching, learning activities and assessment must all point at the same stated outcome, so an ILO promising "design a protocol" cannot be assessed by a recall MCQ. They also connect to Miller's pyramid of clinical competence — knows → knows how → shows how → does — in which Bloom's cognitive levels occupy the lower rungs ("knows", "knows how") while clinical demonstration occupies the upper rungs ("shows how", "does"). Bloom's Taxonomy, published by Bloom and colleagues in 1956 and revised by Anderson and Krathwohl in 2001, classifies educational objectives into levels of increasing cognitive complexity; it is the ladder on which ILOs are written.

3Key concepts, uses and limitations

The revision renamed the levels as verbs and swapped the top two, so creation now sits at the apex. Its deeper change is that it became two-dimensional: a cognitive-process dimension crossed with a knowledge dimension of four content types — factual, conceptual, procedural and metacognitive. A learning outcome is therefore a cell in a grid: "design (create) a graded eccentric loading programme (procedural)" is a different cell from "list the contraindications (factual, remember)". The limitations: the hierarchy is not strictly sequential (a student can create before recalling everything), it can encourage teaching to the lower-order recall levels where most exams quietly live, and the psychomotor and affective domains are harder to specify and measure. Bloom's three domains are cognitive, affective (Krathwohl: receiving, responding, valuing, organising, characterising — attitudes and professionalism) and psychomotor (Simpson/Harrow: perception, set, guided response, mechanism, complex overt response — hands-on skills).

4Answer

Formulating an ILO — a worked example. "By the end of this session, the student will be able to demonstrate the modified Ober's test on a peer without prompting." The verb ("demonstrate") names an observable behaviour; the content ("modified Ober's test") and the standard ("without prompting") make it measurable.

The six objectives of Bloom's Taxonomy, with a physiotherapy example each.

LevelMeaningPhysiotherapy example
1. RememberRecall facts and termsList the six determinants of gait
2. UnderstandExplain ideas in one's own wordsExplain the gate-control theory of pain
3. ApplyUse a rule in a new situationApply the Fick equation to an exercise prescription
4. AnalyseDraw connections and decomposeDifferentiate neuropathic from nociceptive pain in a case
5. EvaluateJustify a decision by criteriaAppraise an RCT's methodological quality
6. CreateProduce new workDesign a 6-week rehabilitation protocol for a post-TKR patient

Using the taxonomy. Write each ILO with a verb at the intended level: "list" and "define" sit at remember, "differentiate" at analyse, "construct" or "justify" at create and evaluate — while "know", "understand" and "appreciate" are unmarkable because they cannot be observed. Then align assessment with the outcome: an ILO promising analysis cannot be tested by a recall MCQ.

Conclusion. ILOs are the measurable destinations of a course, written with observable verbs and the SMART structure; Bloom's Taxonomy — the six cognitive levels of remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate and create, with parallel affective and psychomotor domains — supplies those verbs and, with Miller's pyramid and Biggs's constructive alignment, drives competency-based physiotherapy education. An ILO that names an observable action verb, the content and the standard is the unit of competency-based education.

5Recent advances

  • World Physiotherapy (2022) — its curriculum-framework guidance embeds outcome/competency-based education and constructive alignment of outcomes, teaching and assessment.
  • Timmerberg et al. (2022) — position paper arguing that physical therapy should shift to competency-based education, in which learner progression occurs only when competency is demonstrated.
  • APTA/ACAPT (2025) — the CBEPT framework defines 19 entrustable professional activities (EPAs) and 54 competencies across 8 domains of practice for entrance into practice.
  • Redmond et al. (2024) — the EVIBEC learning-outcomes framework maps evidence-based-practice learning outcomes to the 5 A's of EBP and to Bloom's taxonomy.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 6 (a–c).
  2. Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing. 2001 (revision of Bloom 1956).
  3. Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Acad Med. 1990 (Miller's pyramid).
  4. Biggs J. Teaching for Quality Learning at University. (constructive alignment)
  5. World Physiotherapy. Curriculum framework guidance for physiotherapist entry-level education programmes. 2022.
  6. Fitzpatrick JA, Jensen GM, Chesbro SB. Fundamentals of Competency-Based Education in Physical Therapy. J Phys Ther Educ. 2024;38(2).
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper I — Practice, Pedagogy & Research

QP 8129 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Physiotherapy & EBP

  • Definition (World Physiotherapy): develop, maintain, restore maximum movement & function — primary-contact, autonomous, ICF-based.
  • EBP triad: best evidence + clinical expertise + patient values (Sackett); 5 steps: Ask (PICOT) → Acquire (PubMed, PEDro) → Appraise → Apply → Assess.
  • Hierarchy: SR/meta-analysis → RCT → cohort → case-control → cross-sectional → case series → opinion.

2Ethics

  • 4 principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice + World Physiotherapy standards + ICMR 2017.
  • Issues: informed consent, confidentiality, scope of practice, overtreatment, boundaries, documentation, equity, advertising.

3Pilot study

  • Tests the PROCESS (recruitment, protocol, instruments, drop-out, cost) — never the hypothesis; provides SD for sample size; don't pool its data.

4Sampling

  • SRS = equal independent chance (lottery/RNG). Stratified = SRS within strata (guarantees subgroups).
  • Cluster = random groups, all members. Systematic = every k-th after random start. Multi-stage = successive random stages.

5Qualitative research

  • Designs: phenomenology (lived experience), grounded theory (builds theory), ethnography (culture).
  • Purposive sampling → saturation (no new themes). Thematic analysis 6 phases (Braun & Clarke).
  • Trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability (= internal/external validity, reliability, objectivity).

6Energy transfer

  • First law: energy only converted (food → work + heat); ATP ~7.3 kcal/mol; CP shuttle fastest.
  • Systems: ATP-PC 10 s → glycolysis ~2 min → oxidative (unlimited). Efficiency only 20–25%; 1 MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min.

7Weight control

  • Deficit 500–750 kcal/day → 0.5–1 kg/wk; goal 5–10% in 3–6 months.
  • FITT: 150 → 250–300 min/wk moderate aerobic + resistance 2–3 d/wk; Indian waist ≥90/80 cm = abdominal obesity.

8NMES instrumentation

  • Chain: power → oscillator (Hz, µs) → timer (on:off, ramp) → amplifier (mA) → charge-balanced biphasic output → electrodes.
  • Motor: 35–50 Hz, 200–400 µs, duty cycle 1:3–1:5; Russian = 2.5 kHz carrier, 50 bps; large electrode on motor point.

9SPADI psychometrics

  • 13 items (5 pain + 8 disability), each 0–10 → 0–100% (higher = worse).
  • Reliability ICC 0.84–0.94; α 0.86–0.98; MCID ≈ 8–10 points; Hindi/Kannada versions validated.

10ILOs & Bloom

  • ILO = pre-written, SMART, observable action verb ("demonstrate", not "understand").
  • Bloom (revised): remember → understand → apply → analyse → evaluate → create; Miller: knows → knows how → shows → does; constructive alignment (Biggs).
Keep-if-nothing-else: the EBP 5 steps, the 4 ethics principles, T-score-like trio of numbers (7.3 kcal/mol ATP; 500–750 kcal deficit; 1:3–1:5 duty cycle), and Bloom's six verbs in order. These four alone anchor 6 of 10 questions.
