Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the documentation procedure adopted in terms of assessment, management in rehabilitation based on International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1a — history taking, documentation and the ICF framework

★ Memory hook — ICF in four letters: b, s, d, e — Body function, Structure, activity and participation (d), Environment — and personal factors are never coded.

1Introduction

The ICF is the World Health Organization's operational form of the biopsychosocial model: instead of documenting only the disease (ICD), we document what the disease does to the person. Functioning and disability are described as the interaction of a health condition with body functions, body structures, activities, participation, and the environmental and personal factors that surround the patient. This is the core shift examiners look for — from "what is wrong with the knee" to "what the stiff knee does to the farmer who has to squat to work."

2The ICF model — components and structure

Two parts. Part 1 covers functioning and disability with three components: body functions (coded b), body structures (coded s), and activities and participation (coded d). Part 2 covers contextual factors: environmental factors (coded e) and personal factors, which are described but not classified. Every code carries a qualifier from 0 to 4 — no impairment to complete impairment — so d450.2 means moderate difficulty walking.

Fig 1 — the ICF map: health condition on top, the three functioning boxes in the middle, contextual factors at the bottom. Drawing exactly this earns the component mark in under sixty seconds.

3Assessment and documentation — the procedure

Take a post-stroke patient in a district hospital OPD. History and examination findings are first organised by level: body function and structure — b730 muscle power impairment 2, spasticity b735.1, shoulder subluxation s73016; activity — d450 walking with quadripod, moderate limitation; participation — d920 recreation and d850 remunerative employment severely restricted. Contextual factors: e310 immediate family is supportive (facilitator, +3), e140 work products absent, e115 assistive products unavailable in the village (barrier). Each finding gets a code plus a qualifier — that pairing is what turns a case sheet into ICF documentation.

4Answer

Write SMART goals at each level: body level — improve shoulder abduction power by one MRC grade in six weeks; activity — independent walking for 200 metres with a stick by week eight; participation — return to light farm work by twelve weeks. Every intervention column must cite the level it targets, and every re-assessment must use the same qualifiers so the change is measurable. Link standardized scales to codes: the SPADI documents shoulder pain and disability, a 10-metre walk test documents d450.

The ICF prevents impairment-only physiotherapy, gives a common language to the whole rehabilitation team, and justifies goal setting that the family understands. In the Indian context it forces us to document environmental barriers — a house with a squat toilet, a workplace with no seating, a bus with a high step — which is exactly what decides whether our exercise programme translates to real life. Never describe ICF as a "classification of disability" — the C is functioning AND disability, and omitting environmental factors is the commonest reason candidates lose marks.

5Recent advances

  • WHO (2020) — released the web-based ICF 2020 version, merging the child-and-youth version (ICF-CY) back into the main ICF so it is now the single official classification for documenting functioning across the lifespan.
  • WHO (2019) — aligned the ICF with ICD-11 and ICHI through shared extension codes, letting physiotherapists link functioning data to diagnosis and intervention data across health information systems.
  • WHO (2017) — launched the Rehabilitation 2030: Call for Action, making functioning (ICF) the third health indicator alongside mortality and morbidity and prioritising scale-up of rehabilitation services worldwide.
  • Cieza et al. (2004) — developed the Comprehensive (78-category) and Brief (35-category) ICF Core Sets for low back pain, giving physiotherapists a standard set of functioning categories to structure assessment, goal-setting and outcome evaluation.
  • Kirschneck et al. (2011) — a Delphi validation with 84 physical therapists in 32 countries confirmed the Comprehensive ICF Core Set for low back pain for body structures, activities/participation and environmental factors, but flagged several body-function categories that still need adding.

6References

  1. World Health Organization. International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF). Geneva: WHO; 2001.
  2. World Health Organization. ICF web version 2020 (ICF-CY merged into ICF). Geneva: WHO.
  3. World Physiotherapy. Standards of Physiotherapy Practice. London: World Physiotherapy; 2023.
  4. Roach KE, Budiman-Mak E, Songsiridej N, Lertratanakul Y. Development of a Shoulder Pain and Disability Index. Arthritis Care & Research, 1991.
  5. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. F.A. Davis.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Define Competency. Add a note on Competency-Based Physiotherapy Education.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1b — competencies and the physiotherapy education framework

★ Memory hook — Competency = habitual + judicious + Knowledge, Skills, Attitudes; CBPE builds the curriculum backwards from the graduate outcome, and Miller's pyramid ends at "does."

1Introduction

Competency is the habitual and judicious integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes displayed in real clinical practice. Three domains, never two — a therapist who can pass a written test on gait training but cannot communicate the plan to an anxious grandfather is knowledgeable, not competent. Add the word habitual: one lucky performance on exam day is not competency; it must be reproducible over time and across situations.

2Background and principles of competency-based education

Competency-Based Physiotherapy Education (CBPE) turns the curriculum inside-out: instead of “we taught ten lectures on electrotherapy, therefore the student is ready,” it declares the desired graduate outcome first — the competent entry-level clinician — and designs teaching, learning and assessment backwards from it. This is constructive alignment. Content is organised into competencies with milestones that state observable behaviours, mapped to Bloom's revised taxonomy verbs: a student must be able to assess, plan, apply and evaluate — not merely describe. Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) convert competencies into real clinical units of work such as “assess and manage a patient with mechanical low-back pain under supervision.”

3Curriculum, outcomes and assessment

George Miller's pyramid is the framework examiners expect here. At the base, “knows” is tested by MCQs; “knows how” by case discussions and vivas; “shows how” by OSCE stations on simulated patients; and only the apex — “does” — is assessed at the patient's side through workplace-based assessment and direct observation. In CBPE the dominant assessment becomes the apex, feedback becomes continuous and formative rather than a single summative verdict, and progression is by demonstrated achievement, not time served.

Fig 2 — Miller's pyramid with the matching assessment tool beside each tier. Note the arrow: CBPE is judged at the apex, "does," on real patients.

4Answer

Traditional education versus CBPE — the contrast the question wants:

FeatureTraditional physiotherapy educationCompetency-based education
Starting pointContent and syllabus coverageDesired graduate outcome (competency)
ProgressionBy time served (fixed semesters)By demonstrated achievement (flexible time)
AssessmentSummative knowledge tests dominateWorkplace-based; apex of Miller's pyramid
FeedbackEnd-of-course verdictContinuous, formative, developmental
Learner rolePassive recipientActive, self-directed, accountable

Advantages of CBPE: transparency of outcomes, learner-centred flexibility (a student may take twelve weeks or sixteen to master a skill), early clinical exposure, and assessment that mirrors actual practice. Challenges in India: batch sizes of sixty-plus make individualised feedback expensive; faculty need training in direct observation; workplace assessment demands clinical infrastructure that colleges attached to small hospitals struggle to provide; and a national competency framework for physiotherapy is still maturing, though the CBME model adopted for MBBS gives a ready template.

Conclusion. Competency is the habitual integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes; competency-based physiotherapy education designs the curriculum backwards from that graduate outcome, aligns teaching and assessment to it, and judges the learner at the apex of Miller's pyramid — on real patients, not on paper. The definition must contain all three domains and the word habitual, and CBPE must be linked to assessment at the apex — quoting Bloom's verbs (assess, evaluate, create) picks up easy marks.

5Recent advances

  • Zainuldin & Tan (2021) — developed five core entry-level Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) for the Singapore undergraduate physiotherapy programme, mapped to five competency domains.
  • Baehler et al. (2023) — a Bern University of Applied Sciences pilot developed musculoskeletal EPAs for the clinical training of physiotherapy students and validated the prototypes with the EQual Rubric for EPAs.
  • Merolli et al. (2025) — an international Delphi study produced the first consensus set of nine EPAs and 56 specifications for digital physiotherapy practice, with informed consent for digital health rated highest.
  • Shumba et al. (2024) — used a scoping review mapped to the WHO Rehabilitation Competency Framework to propose a context-specific competency framework for a resource-limited undergraduate physiotherapy programme in Namibia.
  • Ten Cate & Taylor (2021) — AMEE Guide No. 140 standardised how an EPA should be described and entrusted, giving a common language across the health professions.

6References

  1. Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Academic Medicine, 1990.
  2. Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing (Bloom revised).
  3. World Physiotherapy. Physiotherapist Education Framework and Standards of Practice.
  4. Zainuldin R, Tan HY. Development of entrustable professional activities for a physiotherapy undergraduate programme in Singapore. Physiotherapy. 2021;112:64–71.
  5. Ten Cate O, Taylor DR. The recommended description of an entrustable professional activity: AMEE Guide No. 140. Medical Teacher. 2021;43(10):1106–1114.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe various methods of sampling and sample size determination.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3a — sampling methods and sample size in research methodology

★ Memory hook — No frame, no probability sample; and n = Z² p q / d² with p = 0.5, d = 0.05 gives 384.

1Introduction

We study a sample because studying the entire population of Indian knee-osteoarthritis patients is impossible — but the sample must behave like the population it came from. Define the target population, the accessible population, and the sampling frame — the complete, reachable list of population members from which you actually draw. In India the frame is the honest weak link: electoral rolls miss migrants, hospital registers miss those who never reach hospital, and every such gap is selection bias before your study begins.

2Sampling methods — probability and non-probability

Probability sampling — every subject has a known, non-zero chance. Simple random sampling: every member has an equal chance; use random number tables or software; unbiased but needs a complete frame and spreads travel over wide geography. Systematic sampling: pick every k-th person from a list after a random start — convenient for OPD registration queues. Stratified sampling: split the frame into layers — sex, age band, urban or rural — and sample within each, guaranteeing that a minority group is not wiped out by chance. Cluster sampling: randomly select whole clusters — villages, schools, anganwadi centres — then study everyone inside; cheapest for community surveys in dispersed rural populations, at the price of design effect and lower precision. Multistage sampling stacks these: random districts, then random PHCs, then households.

Non-probability sampling — practical, but generalisation dies. Convenience sampling: whoever walks into your OPD that month — the default of most Indian student dissertations, acceptable for pilot studies only. Purposive sampling: you deliberately select information-rich cases, the backbone of qualitative work. Snowball sampling: each enrolled subject recruits peers from the same hidden network — essential when studying stigmatised groups such as drug users. Quota sampling: fill fixed numbers in each category for speed. Consecutive sampling: every eligible patient during a defined window — the least-biased clinical option and always worth naming.

Fig 3 — the sampling tree. Draw the frame in the middle: examiners specifically check whether you know that probability methods die without a complete frame.

3Sample size determination

Sample size is not a tradition of thirty per group; it is calculated from four inputs: the expected effect size or prevalence, the acceptable margin of error d, the confidence level (usually 95%, Z = 1.96), and the power (usually 80%, Z = 0.84) against the assumed type II error. For a proportion or prevalence: n = Z² × p × q ÷ d² — with no prior estimate, take p = 0.5, d = 0.05, giving 384, the number behind most Indian prevalence surveys. For comparing two means: n = 2 × Z² × s² ÷ (effect size)², where the standardised difference is Cohen's d. Add 10 to 20 percent for attrition, and for cluster designs multiply by the design effect. Too small a study misses a true effect; too large wastes scarce resources and exposes more subjects than needed to risk — both are ethical failures, which links this question to Unit 2.

4Answer

Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (false alarm), guarded by the significance level alpha; type II error is missing a real effect, guarded by power — one minus beta. Report that you calculated sample size before, not after, data collection: a post-hoc power justification reads as an excuse. In ICMR-funded multicentric trials the statistician finalises this calculation in the protocol stage — say so, and you sound like a researcher rather than a student. The formula for a proportion, with the worked figure of 384, is the single highest-yield fact in this unit, and always write "sample size was calculated for the primary outcome," because a study powered for one outcome is not powered for all of them.

5Recent advances

  • Faul et al. (2007) — G*Power 3 made a priori power analysis free and routine, covering the t, F, chi-square, z and exact test families and becoming the standard tool for sample-size calculation in physiotherapy research.
  • Fernández Hernando et al. (2024) — an analysis of 100 physical-therapy trials found about one-third reported no sample-size calculation and only 59% both calculated and achieved their target sample size, exposing a persistent methodological weakness.
  • Bae & Song (2025) — a systematic review of 285 exercise RCTs in older, musculoskeletal and neurological patients showed effect size was reported in only 22–27% and up to 30% reported none of the four sample-size elements (alpha, power, effect size, attrition).
  • Pawel & Held (2024) — Bayesian sample-size determination matured, with closed-form formulas and the R package bfpwr allowing trial design based on Bayes factors instead of p-value power.

6References

  1. Hulley SB, Cummings SR, Browner WS, Grady DG, Newman TB. Designing Clinical Research. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
  2. Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics. CRC Press.
  3. ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
  4. Serdar CC, Cihan M, Yücel D, Serdar MA. Sample size, power and effect size revisited: simplified and practical approaches in pre-clinical, clinical and laboratory studies. Biochemia Medica. 2021;31(1):010502.
  5. Faul F, Erdfelder E, Lang AG, Buchner A. G*Power 3: a flexible statistical power analysis program for the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences. Behavior Research Methods. 2007;39(2):175–191.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Explain the ethical principles in practice of physiotherapy in a hospital and community.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 2a — World Physiotherapy standards, ICMR guidelines and ethical issues

★ Memory hook — Four principles: Autonomy, Beneficence, Non-maleficence, Justice — then ask how each one changes in a ward versus a village square.

1Introduction

Ethics in physiotherapy rests on two legs: the four prima facie principles of Beauchamp and Childress, and the professional codes that convert them into rules of conduct — the World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice and, for research and community programmes in India, the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines 2017. In your answer, principles give the philosophy and codes give the enforceable behaviour; quoting both is what lifts the answer from a philosophy essay to a professional one.

2The four principles with physiotherapy examples

Autonomy: the patient's right to decide — exercised through informed consent, truth-telling about the diagnosis, and respect for refusal; an OPD patient may decline a passive-mobilisation technique and we document and respect it. Beneficence: act for the patient's benefit — choose the exercise programme with the best evidence for that person, not the most profitable for the clinic. Non-maleficence: do no harm — screen for red flags, avoid over-pressure on osteoporotic spines, apply a risk-benefit justification for every modality. Justice: fairness in distribution — equal quality of care for a ward patient and a private cubicle patient, transparent fees, no discrimination by caste, religion, gender, HIV status or ability to pay.

Fig 4 — the four-quadrant ethics map with the physiotherapy hook under each principle; the examiner asks for examples, and this figure is your memory palace.

3Hospital practice — consent, confidentiality and boundaries

In hospital: obtain consent before the first assessment and again for any change of plan, in the patient's language, and remember a signature without understanding is not consent. Guard confidentiality — no case discussions in hospital corridors, no patient photos on personal phones, and digital records protected as the ICMR data-protection expectations require. Maintain professional boundaries — no personal relationships with patients under care. Document every session honestly; the case sheet is the ethical record that protects the patient and you. Practise within your scope: refer onwards to an orthopaedician or a physician when red flags exceed physiotherapy. Follow infection control, be truthful about fees and likely outcomes, and do not promise cures — "guaranteed pain relief in three sittings" is an ethical breach, not marketing.

4Answer

In the community — health camps, school screening, industrial ergonomic visits — the same principles apply but the machinery is weaker. Voluntariness must be real: a free camp attended by the whole village because the employer sanctioned leave is not entirely voluntary. Cultural and religious sensitivity decides whether an exercise programme is followed: prescribing knee flexion postures where squatting is required for daily life is poor rehabilitation. Justice dominates community work: reaching patients who cannot reach us, and using ICMR 2017 standards when the programme involves data collection — ethical committee approval, anonymised records, and benefit flowing back to the community studied, not only to the researchers. The distinction marks come from the hospital versus community contrast — consent machinery, confidentiality machinery and justice issues all change when the patient is in a village square rather than on a plinth.

5Recent advances

  • World Physiotherapy (2023) — re-approved its merged policy statement Ethical principles and the responsibilities of physiotherapists and member organisations, listing eight ethical principles and requiring every member organisation to hold a code of ethics with monitoring and disciplinary procedures.
  • World Physiotherapy (2023) — the Standards of Physiotherapy Practice set national practice standards in ethical and professional practice, communication, evidence-based practice and quality improvement.
  • World Physiotherapy (2021) — its regulation policy promotes a "right-touch", harm-prevention model of professional regulation rather than purely reactive complaints handling.
  • Merolli et al. (2025) — the international Delphi on digital-health EPAs for physiotherapy makes "obtaining informed consent" for digital health the highest-rated competency, so ethics is now being written into tele-rehabilitation standards.

6References

  1. ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
  2. World Physiotherapy. Standards of Physiotherapy Practice. London; 2023.
  3. Sackett DL, Straus SE, Richardson WS, Rosenberg W, Haynes RB. Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM. Churchill Livingstone.
  4. World Physiotherapy. Policy statement: Ethical principles and the responsibilities of physiotherapists and member organisations. London: World Physiotherapy; 2023.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Explain the instrumentation for neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 5b — NMES instrumentation and electrotherapeutic currents

★ Memory hook — Signal chain: Transformer → Rectifier/filter → Oscillator (555) → Output stage with coupling transformer → Patient.

1Introduction

Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) applies controlled electrical pulses through surface electrodes to produce a muscle contraction for therapeutic gain — strengthening, atrophy prevention, re-education and the muscle pump. The instrument must generate a safe, controllable, balanced pulse train and deliver it to the motor point of the target muscle; understanding its instrumentation means following the current from the mains socket to the skin.

2Physiology

NMES does not excite the muscle fibre directly; it depolarises the motor axon under the cathode, and the action potential travelling to the neuromuscular junction produces contraction exactly as voluntary effort does. Because it bypasses the voluntary motor drive, even a patient with upper-motor-neuron weakness contracts — but note the reversal of recruitment order: electrical stimulation recruits large, fast type II axons before small type I axons, the opposite of the Henneman size principle, and the reason NMES fatigues muscle faster than voluntary work.

3Pathophysiology

The clinical reason to reach for NMES is the failure of normal activation. In upper-motor-neuron lesions — stroke, incomplete spinal cord injury — the muscle and its peripheral nerve are intact but the descending drive is lost, so surface stimulation can still contract the muscle. In disuse and immobilisation the muscle atrophies and loses strength and mass; NMES arrests this. In denervation there is no axon to depolarise, so ordinary short pulses fail and the muscle fibre itself must be excited with long, tens-of-milliseconds triangular or exponential pulses. The reversed type II recruitment also explains the rapid fatigue seen with prolonged tetanic contractions.

4Answer

The signal chain, block by block. The mains at 230 V AC enters a step-down transformer, is rectified to DC and smoothed by a filter to give a safe, stable low-voltage supply. This powers the oscillator / timer — classically a 555-type timer — which generates the pulse train and sets frequency, phase duration and on–off timing. The oscillator output drives the output stage, a transistorised amplifier that raises current to the therapeutic level, usually through a coupling (isolation) transformer that separates the patient from the mains — the safety heart of the instrument. Finally the current reaches the skin through electrodes placed over the motor point of the target muscle.

Waveform and the clinician's five dials. The waveform of choice is a symmetrical or asymmetrical biphasic pulsed current, because balanced charge leaves no net DC component and prevents iontophoresis-like skin irritation and burns. Frequency: 2–10 Hz twitches the muscle for drainage and the muscle pump; 20–50 Hz produces tetanic contraction for strengthening; 80–100 Hz is used for spasm inhibition at the cost of fast fatigue. Phase duration: 200–400 µs sits over the strength–duration curve's comfortable motor threshold for innervated muscle. Duty cycle (on:off) is 1:5 in early reconditioning and about 1:1 for strengthening — more off-time means less fatigue. Ramp-up and ramp-down of 100–300 ms let the patient tolerate higher amplitude, and amplitude is turned to the maximum tolerated, aiming for a strong, comfortable tetanic contraction.

Electrodes, safety and contraindications. Electrode size is matched to muscle bulk — larger electrodes lower current density and improve comfort; placement over the motor point lowers the threshold. Skin must be prepped and impedance checked; broken current paths cause burns. Contraindications and precautions: cardiac pacemakers and implanted devices, the carotid sinus, the pregnant uterus, active deep vein thrombosis, areas of active malignancy, and sensory loss where the patient cannot report excessive current.

Instrument types — one line each. Conventional NMES stimulators; Russian current (2.5 kHz carrier burst-modulated at 50 bursts/s, for strengthening); functional electrical stimulation (stimulation synchronised to a task such as foot-drop walking); TENS (sensory-level sibling for pain); and stimulators for denervated muscle, which must deliver long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds — often triangular or exponential.

Conclusion. NMES instrumentation is one chain — transformer → oscillator/timer → output amplifier → isolation → electrodes → motor point — whose five dials map directly onto physiology. The therapist who understands each block knows exactly which control changes which physiological outcome, which is the whole point of studying instrumentation.

Fig 5 — the four-block signal chain with the five parameters listed beside it. Draw this chain and the examiner can see the current physically travelling; that is the whole instrumentation mark.

5Recent advances

  • Maffiuletti (2010) — the definitive review of NMES physiology and methodology recommended biphasic 100–400 microsecond pulses at 50–100 Hz and the highest tolerated intensity to maximise evoked force, and showed that evoked tension rather than current parameters drives effectiveness.
  • Gobbo et al. (2011) — showed that locating the muscle motor point with a pen electrode rather than using anatomical charts maximises evoked torque and metabolic response while minimising current and discomfort, now a recommended electrode-placement step.
  • Ackermann et al. (2024) — automated motor-point search within an electrode matrix and garment-based wearable NMES let a device individualise electrode number/size and integrate electrodes into clothing, tackling the commonest cause of failure — poor electrode placement and low compliance.
  • Xu et al. (2024) — a network meta-analysis (23 RCTs, 1312 ventilated adults) found NMES plus physical therapy best for extubation success in critically ill patients, though evidence quality was low.
  • Kourek et al. (2024) — a prospective observational study showed NMES to be safe and feasible in patients on ECMO, extending electrically induced contraction to the sickest ICU patients.

6References

  1. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. F.A. Davis.
  3. Fan D, Zhou H, Cai Y, et al. Efficacy assessment for NMES in improving muscle strength in patients with severe acute pancreatitis complicated by ARDS. Journal of Army Medical University. 2024;46(22):2539–2546.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain the various study designs in research.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3b — research designs, experimental and observational

★ Memory hook — Who allocates the exposure? No → observational; Yes → experimental. Then add the RCT quartet: randomise, conceal, blind, intention-to-treat.

1Introduction

Start with the axis that earns the structure marks: does the investigator allocate the exposure? If not, the design is observational — descriptive (case report, case series, cross-sectional survey) or analytical (case-control, cohort). If yes, the design is experimental — randomised controlled trial, quasi-experiment, pre-experimental pre-post designs, and the single-case (n-of-1) experiment. A second axis is timing: retrospective looks backwards from outcome, prospective looks forward from exposure. Every design below is one cell of this grid; say the grid first.

2Classification and observational designs

Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time point; they give prevalence, not incidence, and cannot prove sequence — useful for a survey of low back pain prevalence among Bengaluru autorickshaw drivers. Case-control studies start from the outcome: past exposure is compared between cases and controls, yielding an odds ratio; efficient for rare outcomes like transient brachial plexopathy, but memory bias is the toll. Cohort studies start from exposure and follow forward for the outcome — relative risk, temporal sequence established, the ethical design when withholding treatment is impossible; the price is time, expense and loss to follow-up. Case reports and series generate hypotheses, one patient at a time.

3Experimental and qualitative designs

The randomised controlled trial is the reference standard: randomisation distributes known and unknown confounders equally between groups, concealed allocation prevents selection bias, blinding of patient, therapist and assessor prevents expectation bias, and an intention-to-treat analysis preserves the randomisation. State the PICO question explicitly — population, intervention, comparison, outcome — and the design becomes obvious rather than memorised. Below the RCT sit quasi-experimental designs (allocation by ward or by week, when randomising individuals is impossible), pre-post single-group designs (no control, only a hypothesis), the single-case experimental design with repeated baseline phases — a clinician's research method for one patient — and crossover trials, where each patient is their own control and a washout period separates phases.

Fig 6 — the evidence pyramid: the level of evidence ladder you climb when grading any published answer. Higher means better protection against bias, not automatic truth.

Not every clinical question is answered by numbers. Why patients abandon home programmes, or how families experience stroke caregiving, needs qualitative designs — phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography — analysed by the Braun and Clarke six-phase thematic analysis.

4Answer

Matching the design to the question is itself a research skill: a therapy question wants an RCT or systematic review, a prognosis question wants a cohort, a diagnostic accuracy question wants a cross-sectional comparison against a gold standard, and a meaning question wants qualitative work. For every design, give one physiotherapy example and one statistic it produces — odds ratio for case-control, relative risk for cohort, and the phrase "randomisation plus concealment plus blinding plus intention-to-treat" for the RCT. The evidence pyramid ranks systematic reviews above RCTs above cohort above case-control above case reports: higher means better protection against bias, not automatic truth. Designs described without their bias controls read like a menu, not an answer.

5Recent advances

  • SPIRIT–CONSORT Executive Group (2024) — harmonised the reporting checklists for trial protocols and trial reports (SPIRIT 2024 and CONSORT 2024) into a single aligned set (34 and 30 items), reflecting data-sharing and open-science expectations.
  • Page et al. (2021) — the PRISMA 2020 statement replaced PRISMA 2009 with a revised 27-item checklist, expanded flow diagrams and an abstract checklist, and is now the standard for reporting systematic reviews of physiotherapy interventions.
  • Maher et al. (2003) — established the reliability of the PEDro scale, the physiotherapy-specific 11-item tool for rating RCT quality that now underpins the Physiotherapy Evidence Database and most physiotherapy systematic reviews.
  • Dimairo et al. (2020) — the Adaptive designs CONSORT Extension (ACE) guides transparent reporting of pre-planned changes such as sample-size re-estimation and early stopping.

6References

  1. Hulley SB, Cummings SR, Browner WS, Grady DG, Newman TB. Designing Clinical Research. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
  2. Sackett DL, Straus SE, Richardson WS, Rosenberg W, Haynes RB. Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM. Churchill Livingstone.
  3. Herbert R, Jamtvedt G, Mead J, Hagen KB. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy. Elsevier.
  4. Braun V, Clarke V. Using Thematic Analysis in Psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 2006.
  5. Methods used to develop the SPIRIT 2024 and CONSORT 2024 Statements. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 2024.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Discuss in brief parametric and non-parametric tests.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3c — biostatistics: parametric and non-parametric tests

★ Memory hook — Every parametric test has a rank twin: paired t ↔ Wilcoxon; unpaired t ↔ Mann-Whitney U; ANOVA ↔ Kruskal-Wallis; Pearson ↔ Spearman.

1Introduction

Parametric tests assume that the data follow a specific distribution — the normal, Gaussian curve — and estimate its parameters, mean and standard deviation. Their four assumptions: the normality assumption, data measured on interval or ratio scale, homogeneity of variance across compared groups, and independence of observations. Non-parametric tests make no such distributional assumption — hence "distribution-free" — and work on ranks, so they tolerate ordinal scales like pain scores and skewed data like hospital stay or income. Verify normality in your answer with the Shapiro-Wilk test, or by eyeballing the histogram and Q-Q plot; naming an actual check is worth more than reciting the assumption.

2Parametric tests — assumptions and common tests

One group versus a known value: one-sample t-test. Two paired measurements — pain before and after ten sittings of interferential therapy: paired t-test. Two independent groups — conventional exercise versus physiotherapist-supervised exercise in two OPD cohorts: unpaired (independent) t-test. Three or more independent groups: one-way ANOVA, with a post-hoc test such as Tukey to find which pair differs. Repeated measurements across time: repeated-measures ANOVA. Relationship between two continuous variables: Pearson's correlation coefficient r. Each test outputs a p-value and, in modern reporting, a confidence interval — say "p less than 0.05 means evidence against the null, not proof of a large effect."

3Non-parametric tests — the rank twins

Every parametric test has a rank-based twin. Paired setting: the sign test (direction only) and the more powerful Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Two independent groups: Mann-Whitney U test. Three or more groups: Kruskal-Wallis H test. Repeated measures: Friedman test. Correlation: Spearman's rho. For categorical data the chi-square test — goodness of fit, and independence in a contingency table — belongs here too, with Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts fall below five.

Fig 7 — the choosing tree: the question box in the middle is where marks live; the test names are just leaves.

4Answer

Decision path: normality and interval data with comparable variances choose parametric; ordinal, ranked, skewed or outlier-heavy data choose non-parametric. Both paths must still respect independence and the pairing structure of the design — a paired test on unpaired data is a more serious error than choosing the wrong family. If the data look nearly normal, prefer the parametric test: on normal data it is the more powerful, and on mildly non-normal data the rank tests retain roughly 95 percent of that efficiency, so little is lost either way. The commonest viva trap: applying a paired t-test to two independent groups, or an unpaired test to before-after data — always state the design first, then the test. Write the answer as a paired table — parametric test on the left, its non-parametric twin on the right — and add one line on why you chose each: "VAS pain is ordinal, so Wilcoxon signed-rank."

5Recent advances

  • Vovk & Wang (2024) — the e-value / e-test framework offers an alternative to p-values, with non-parametric e-tests of symmetry and a Pitman-type efficiency measure for rank tests.
  • Bertanha & Chung (2023) — extended permutation tests to parameters estimated at root-n or slower rates (JASA), giving exact size in finite samples while retaining full asymptotic power.
  • Terwee et al. (2007) — proposed explicit quality criteria for the measurement properties of health-status questionnaires (content validity, reliability, responsiveness, interpretability), the basis of the COSMIN standards used to judge physiotherapy outcome measures.
  • Bland & Altman (1986) — introduced the limits-of-agreement method for assessing agreement between two measurement methods, now the standard approach for quantifying measurement error in physiotherapy outcome measurement.

6References

  1. Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics. CRC Press.
  2. Hulley SB, Cummings SR, Browner WS, Grady DG, Newman TB. Designing Clinical Research. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
  3. Mukhopadhyay S, Wang K. A nonparametric approach to high-dimensional k-sample comparison problems. Biometrika. 2020;107(3):555–572.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Considerations for exercise prescription in obesity.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4c — exercise prescription across conditions and body compositions

★ Memory hook — Asian Indian cutoffs: obesity BMI ≥ 25, central obesity waist 90 cm (men) / 80 cm (women) — then prescribe FITT with numbers.

1Introduction

Obesity is excess body fat with health risk, and for Asian Indians the thresholds arrive early: by the Misra et al. JAPI 2009 consensus, obesity is a body mass index of 25 or more (overweight 23 to 24.9) — not the Western cutoff of 30 — and central obesity is a waist circumference of 90 cm or more in men and 80 cm or more in women. Indians also develop the "thin-fat" phenotype: metabolic risk at lower BMI, which is why we screen and treat earlier and why quoting these Indian numbers earns the definition mark over reciting Western values.

2Physiology

Exercise works on both sides of the energy-balance equation. Each activity has a metabolic cost measured in METs — brisk walking is about 4, cycling about 8 — so the calorie cost of a session is calculable and can be matched to the calorie content of a chapati. Resistance training adds a second lever: each kilogram of muscle gained raises resting metabolic rate, and exercise during weight loss preserves lean mass that dieting alone squanders. Exercise also improves insulin sensitivity, cardiorespiratory fitness and appetite regulation, benefits that accrue even when the weighing scale barely moves.

3Pathophysiology

Before prescribing, review the comorbidities that make obesity a disease. Type 2 diabetes and its medication timing: exercise after an insulin or sulfonylurea dose risks hypoglycaemia — advise carrying glucose and adjusting the dose with the physician. Hypertension: record resting blood pressure and defer if 180/110 or above until controlled. Dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, and painful knees or low back from the mechanical load all modify the programme. Stratify cardiovascular risk — the apparently healthy obese adult can begin moderate activity without testing, while symptomatic patients or those planning vigorous exercise need medical clearance.

4Answer

Dose it like a drug, using the FITT principle grid plus volume and progression. Frequency: aerobic exercise on five days a week (or every day if lighter), resistance on two to three non-consecutive days. Intensity: moderate, 40 to 60 percent of heart-rate reserve, or a talk-test pace where the patient can still converse, rating of perceived exertion 11 to 13 on the Borg 6-to-20 scale. Time: 30 to 60 minutes daily, accumulated in bouts of at least ten minutes, building to the guideline volume of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity weekly. Type: load-friendly aerobic choices first — brisk walking, stationary cycling, swimming or aqua exercise (buoyancy unloads the knees), later progressing to jogging; plus large-muscle resistance training. Quantify energy cost in METs so the patient can see that walking thirty minutes burns roughly the calories of one chapati, and that diet must change in parallel: exercise alone rarely outpaces a calorie surplus. Baseline measures to document: waist circumference, resting heart rate and blood pressure, a six-minute walk test, and functional joint status.

Fig 8 — the FITT pillars with a number against each; the bottom banner is the sentence examiners want to see quoted verbatim.

Progression, safety and the Indian context. Progress volume first, intensity later — add roughly five to ten minutes per fortnight of tolerated walking before touching speed or incline. Protect joints: aquatic exercise, cycles and graded walking paths for the painful knee; cushioned footwear on hard Indian roads; avoid deep squats early. Time outdoor sessions for early morning or evening in Indian heat and humidity, and enforce hydration. Address behaviour, because adherence is the real prescription: written goals, step counters, exercise logs, walking groups for company, and family involvement — in Indian households the kitchen decides the calorie side of the equation, so involve whoever cooks. Reassess monthly with waist circumference and walk time, not the weighing scale alone, and coordinate with a dietitian and physician.

5Recent advances

  • Jakicic et al. (2024) — the ACSM Consensus Statement on Physical Activity and Excess Body Weight and Adiposity confirms benefits are dose-dependent from at least 150 min/week of moderate activity, that no single mode is superior, and that HIIT is not superior to moderate-to-vigorous activity for weight regulation.
  • Oppert et al. (2021) — the EASO Physical Activity Working Group (Obesity Reviews) recommends moderate-intensity aerobic exercise for fat loss (expected loss only 2–3 kg) and resistance training to preserve lean mass, with HIIT only after cardiovascular risk assessment and supervision.
  • O'Donoghue et al. (2021) — a network meta-analysis ranked combined high-intensity aerobic plus high-load resistance training best for reducing abdominal adiposity and improving lean mass and fitness in adults living with obesity.
  • Wewege et al. (2017) — a meta-analysis found HIIT and moderate-intensity continuous training produce similar improvements in body composition in overweight and obese adults, so HIIT is best framed as a time-efficient alternative rather than a superior mode.
  • Wharton et al. (2020) — the Canadian Adult Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline manages obesity as a chronic disease, integrating exercise with nutrition, behavioural therapy and pharmacotherapy, including GLP-1 receptor agonists.

6References

  1. Misra A, Chowbey P, Makkar BM, et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. JAPI, 2009.
  2. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance. Wolters Kluwer.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. F.A. Davis.
  4. Wharton S, Lau DCW, Vallis M, et al. Obesity in adults: a clinical practice guideline. Canadian Medical Association Journal. 2020;192(31):E875–E891.
  5. American College of Sports Medicine. Physical Activity and Excess Body Weight and Adiposity for Adults: ACSM Consensus Statement. 2024.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Differentiate aerobic and anaerobic exercise in terms of energy expenditure.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4a — metabolism and energy systems in exercise

★ Memory hook — Aerobic vs anaerobic in three numbers: 10 seconds : 2 minutes : unlimited — then name the fuel each system burns.

1Introduction

All exercise is powered by ATP, regenerated by three systems on a time-and-intensity clock. The question asks for the difference "in terms of energy expenditure" — so anchor every distinction in ATP: which substrate, how much ATP per glucose molecule, how fast it arrives, and what it costs in oxygen and lactate.

2Physiology

The phosphagen system — stored ATP and creatine phosphate — fuels the first eight to ten seconds of all-out effort anaerobically, without oxygen, without lactate. Anaerobic glycolysis breaks glucose to pyruvate and, when oxygen supply lags demand, ferments it to lactate, regenerating ATP rapidly for roughly ten seconds to two minutes of heavy work. The oxidative (aerobic) system burns carbohydrate and fat in the mitochondria with oxygen, yielding far more ATP per glucose molecule — roughly 32 ATP aerobically versus 2 ATP anaerobically — but only at a slower rate; it dominates from about two minutes onward and supports hours of submaximal work. The systems never switch on and off; they share the load, and the intensity of the exercise decides the share.

3Pathophysiology

When intensity exceeds the aerobic ceiling, hydrogen ions accumulate from anaerobic glycolysis and the muscle fatigues early — this is why the anaerobic share is powerful but brief. At exercise onset, oxidative phosphorylation lags behind demand — the oxygen deficit, covered meanwhile by the phosphagen system and glycolysis. After stopping, oxygen uptake remains raised: EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, the modern name for oxygen debt) repays the phosphagen stores, clears lactate by gluconeogenesis in the liver (the Cori cycle), restores myoglobin, and funds the raised temperature and catecholamine-driven metabolism. Anaerobic exercise produces a large, fast-rising EPOC; aerobic exercise, when severe and prolonged, produces a slower but longer-lasting one — the physiological basis behind interval-training prescriptions for cardiometabolic patients.

4Answer

The differentiation the question asks for. Intensity: aerobic work is moderate, sustainable and below the lactate threshold (roughly 55 to 70 percent of maximal oxygen uptake); anaerobic work is near-maximal, above the lactate threshold, where blood lactate climbs past about 4 mmol per litre. Oxygen demand: aerobic exercise is steady state — uptake meets demand; anaerobic exercise creates an oxygen deficit that must be repaid. Fuel: aerobic uses both carbohydrate and fat (fat burns only in a carbohydrate flame, and only aerobically); anaerobic burns carbohydrate alone. Duration and power: anaerobic delivers high power for seconds to about two minutes; aerobic delivers lower power for minutes to hours. By-products: anaerobic accumulates lactate and hydrogen ions; aerobic yields carbon dioxide and water. Examples a physiotherapist meets daily: a patient rising from a chair once (phosphagen), a stair-climbing test (glycolytic), a six-minute walk test (aerobic).

Fig 9 — the energy timeline every examiner wants: three boxes along the clock, and the crossing lines showing the anaerobic share falling as the aerobic share rises with duration.

Adaptations and testing — close the loop. Aerobic training multiplies mitochondria and aerobic enzymes, raises capillary density and haemoglobin mass, lowers resting heart rate and raises maximal oxygen uptake — tested by graded exercise tests with gas analysis or field tests like the six-minute walk or 20-m shuttle. Anaerobic training enlarges phosphagen stores and glycolytic enzymes and improves hydrogen-ion buffering — tested by the 30-second Wingate anaerobic test or vertical jumps. For our patients, most rehabilitation is aerobic; anaerobic dosing belongs to return-to-sport phases, and the physiotherapist's skill is prescribing on the correct side of the lactate threshold.

5Recent advances

  • Gastin & Suppiah (2026) — an updated systematic review (Sports Medicine) of 102 studies refined the crossover point: the anaerobic and aerobic systems contribute equally at about 79 seconds of maximal exercise, with the anaerobic share predominant only up to roughly 75–80 seconds.
  • Ambaum & Hoppe (2025) — a systematic review found the maximal accumulated oxygen deficit (MAOD) remains the best-evidenced method for quantifying the anaerobic contribution, with critical power (CP) and the PCr-La-O2 method next best.
  • Poole et al. (2016) — established critical power as the fatigue threshold separating the heavy and severe intensity domains, giving physiotherapists a physiological anchor for prescribing aerobic exercise intensity and predicting tolerance.
  • Pontzer et al. (2016) — the constrained total energy expenditure model explains why exercise-induced weight loss is modest: the body compensates by lowering resting metabolic rate and improving movement economy.

6References

  1. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance. Wolters Kluwer.
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier.
  3. Gastin PB. Energy system interaction and relative contribution during maximal exercise. Sports Medicine. 2001;31(10):725–741.
  4. Relative contributions of the anaerobic and aerobic energy systems during maximal exercise: a systematic review. Sports Medicine, 2026.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe electrical stimulation and its effect on various systems.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 5a — electrical properties of muscle and nerve, effects of stimulation

★ Memory hook — One centre box, four targets: Muscle, Nerve, Circulation, Bone/Skin — each target becomes one heading of your answer.

1Introduction

Therapeutic electrical stimulation is the application of controlled electrical current through surface electrodes to excite nerve or muscle and produce a physiological or therapeutic effect. Classify in one line each: by pulse shape (rectangular, triangular, exponential, sinusoidal), by continuity (direct versus pulsed), and by clinical intent — NMES for muscle activation, functional electrical stimulation synchronised to a task, TENS for sensory analgesia, and Russian current for strengthening.

2Physiology

The unifying mechanism for almost all of them: depolarisation of excitable membrane under the cathode when the stimulus crosses the threshold defined by the strength-duration curve.

Effects on muscle — the system we treat most. Stimulation produces contraction whose strength and character follow the frequency: twitches below about 10 to 15 Hz, tetanic contraction from 20 to 50 Hz, and rapid fatigue above that. Recruitment is reversed compared with voluntary effort — large type II motor axons fire first, which makes NMES a useful fast-twitch trainer but an early fatiguer. Used repeatedly, it maintains muscle mass in disuse and immobilisation, retards atrophy after injury or surgery, strengthens weak quadriceps and pelvic floor, re-educates a muscle the patient has "forgotten" to recruit, and pumps venous and lymphatic return through the muscle pump.

Effects on the nervous system — sensory and motor faces. On sensory nerves, low-intensity high-rate stimulation recruits large-diameter afferents and closes the pain gate in the dorsal horn — the mechanism of conventional TENS — while low-rate (2 to 4 Hz) stimulation recruits descending opioid pathways for diffuse analgesia. Stimulated sensory input also improves proprioceptive awareness of a joint. On motor nerves, stimulation preserves axonal excitability and conduction in disuse, and cyclic stimulation of the common peroneal nerve in foot drop is the classic functional application of motor-nerve stimulation.

3Pathophysiology

The dysfunctions stimulation is used to counter are loss of voluntary activation (upper motor neuron weakness), disuse atrophy and immobilisation, and denervation. Denervated muscle needs a different instrument entirely: long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds and triangular or exponential waveforms, because there is no axon to depolarise and the fibre itself must be excited. Rhythmically stimulated muscle also counteracts venous stasis and oedema after injury, and mechanical strain at a fracture site can be used to support delayed union.

4Answer

Effects on circulation and metabolism. Rhythmically stimulated skeletal muscle acts as a peripheral heart: the pumping action drives venous and lymphatic return, reduces oedema after injury and encourages arterial inflow. Large-muscle stimulation raises heart rate and blood pressure because the metabolic demand of contracting muscle triggers sympathetic cardiovascular responses — a consideration in cardiac patients. Local metabolism rises in the stimulated muscle with increased substrate use, and stimulation-induced movement aids nutrition of cartilage and soft tissue in immobilised joints.

Fig 10 — the systems web: a centre box with four targets is the fastest skeleton for "effect on various systems," and each box becomes one h4 of your answer.

Other systems, precautions and conclusion. On bone, mechanical strain generates piezoelectric currents, and clinically applied electrical stimulation is used to support delayed-union fracture healing; on skin, long-standing sensory stimulation can produce trophic changes; smooth muscle and viscera respond poorly to brief pulses, though some bladder and pelvic-floor applications exist. Precautions and contraindications: cardiac pacemakers and implanted electronic devices, stimulation over the carotid sinus, the pregnant uterus, active deep vein thrombosis, malignant tissue and infected areas, and sensory loss where the patient cannot report excess current. In the Indian context, remember the practical system factors — cost, machine availability and adherence — that decide whether a stimulation programme survives beyond the OPD. Conclude with the physiotherapist's principle: electrical stimulation is an adjunct that activates the tissue; the retraining still comes from exercise and function.

5Recent advances

  • Li et al. (2025) — a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs showed NMES added to standard physical therapy significantly improves quadriceps strength after ACL surgery, with the greatest gains when started within one week of surgery.
  • Kern & Carraro (2014) — home-based functional electrical stimulation (the Vienna strategy) has been shown to rebuild permanently denervated quadriceps — increased cross-sectional area and force output after two years — using large electrodes and long pulses.
  • Arora et al. (2020) — a Cochrane review (20 RCTs, 913 participants) found electrical stimulation probably increases the proportion and rate of pressure-ulcer healing (moderate-certainty evidence), supporting its use as an adjunct in wound care.
  • Nascimento et al. (2020) — a meta-analysis of 11 trials (1135 participants) showed continuous functional electrical stimulation significantly improves walking speed after stroke, with effects equivalent to an ankle-foot orthosis for foot drop.
  • Reichenbach et al. (2022) — the ETRELKA randomised trial found TENS was no better than placebo TENS for knee osteoarthritis pain, a conclusive negative result that redirected therapists toward exercise and other modalities.

6References

  1. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. F.A. Davis.
  3. ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
  4. The effect of electrical stimulation in critical patients: a meta-analysis. Frontiers in Neurology, 2024.
  5. Carraro U, et al. Home-based functional electrical stimulation of human permanently denervated muscles: diagnostics, management, results and byproducts revisited 2020. Diagnostics. 2020;10(8):529.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper I

QP 8129 · 19-May-2025 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1ICF documentation

  • WHO 2001; functioning AND disability; codes b, s, d, e; personal factors never coded.
  • Qualifiers 0 to 4 = no to complete problem; assessment documents impairment + activity + participation + context.
  • Management = SMART goals written at each ICF level, same qualifiers repeated at re-assessment.

2Competency and CBPE

  • Definition: habitual + judicious + knowledge, skills, attitudes — all three, always.
  • Miller: knows → knows how → shows how → does; apex = workplace assessment on real patients.
  • CBPE = outcomes first, constructive alignment, EPAs, milestones, Bloom's verbs, progression by demonstration not time.

3Sampling and sample size

  • Frame = the actual list you draw from; no frame, no probability sampling.
  • Probability: simple random, systematic (every k-th), stratified (layers), cluster (villages), multistage; non-probability: convenience, purposive, quota, snowball, consecutive.
  • n = Z²pq/d²; p = 0.5, d = 0.05 gives 384; power 80%, add 10–20% attrition.

4Ethics

  • Four principles: autonomy (consent), beneficence, non-maleficence, justice (equity).
  • Hospital: consent, confidentiality, boundaries, documentation; community: voluntariness, culture, data ethics.
  • Codes: World Physiotherapy Standards + ICMR 2017 for research and community programmes.

5NMES instrumentation

  • Signal chain: transformer → rectifier/smoothing → oscillator (555) → output stage with coupling transformer → patient.
  • Parameters: 20–50 Hz, phase duration 200–400 µs, duty cycle 1:1 to 1:5, ramp 100–300 ms, amplitude max tolerated.
  • Biphasic balanced = no net charge = no burn; denervated muscle needs tens of ms triangular pulses.

6Study designs

  • Investigator allocates? No = observational (cross-sectional → prevalence; case-control → odds ratio; cohort → relative risk); yes = experimental (RCT, quasi, n-of-1, crossover).
  • RCT quality quartet: randomise, conceal, blind, intention-to-treat.
  • Pyramid: systematic reviews over RCTs over cohort over case-control over case reports.

7Parametric vs non-parametric

  • Parametric needs: normality, interval/ratio, homogeneity of variance, independence; check with Shapiro-Wilk.
  • Twins: paired t ↔ Wilcoxon; unpaired t ↔ Mann-Whitney U; ANOVA ↔ Kruskal-Wallis; repeated ANOVA ↔ Friedman; Pearson ↔ Spearman; categories → chi-square.
  • Match the test to the pairing structure first — wrong pairing is the bigger sin.

8Exercise in obesity

  • Asian Indian cutoffs (JAPI 2009): obesity BMI 25 and above; waist 90 cm men, 80 cm women.
  • FITT: 5 d/wk aerobic, 40–60% HRR (RPE 11–13), 30–60 min in 10-min bouts, 150–300 min/wk; resistance 2–3 d/wk.
  • Insulin + exercise = hypoglycaemia risk; protect knees; aqua and cycling; involve the family kitchen.

9Aerobic vs anaerobic

  • ATP-PC 0–10 s; glycolysis 10 s–2 min, lactate ↑; oxidative beyond 2 min, fat burns only aerobically.
  • 2 ATP per glucose anaerobic versus roughly 32 aerobic; lactate threshold about 4 mmol/L.
  • EPOC = old oxygen debt: restore phosphagens, clear lactate (Cori cycle), raised temperature and catecholamines.

10Electrical stimulation on systems

  • Muscle: type II recruited first (reversed order), tetany 20–50 Hz, atrophy arrest; denervated needs long pulses.
  • Nerve: pain gate via large afferents; peroneal stimulation in foot drop.
  • Circulation: muscle pump drives venous/lymphatic return; bone: piezoelectric, delayed-union healing; pacemaker and carotid sinus are hard contraindications.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall — the four ethics principles, the 384 sample-size figure, Miller's pyramid order, FITT with numbers, and the 20–50 Hz / 200–400 µs NMES pair.
