  • Indian practice: ask for old prescriptions and reports (patients rarely carry them), and confirm the timeline against a festival or harvest calendar rather than exact dates.
  • Red flags to hunt in every history: night pain unrelated to position, unexplained weight loss, fever, history of carcinoma, trauma in the elderly, progressive neurological deficit, and loss of bladder or bowel control (a cauda equina emergency).
  • Yellow flags to screen: fear-avoidance beliefs, low mood, poor outcome expectations — they predict chronicity better than any imaging finding. This screening decides whether we treat or refer.
  • ICMR ethical guidance: what a patient tells us is confidential information held in trust, not gossip for the OPD corridor.
  • Record findings under the WHO ICF: body functions and structures (restricted shoulder abduction, weak quadriceps), activity (cannot comb hair, cannot squat), participation (unable to attend office, cannot lift the child), environmental factors (lives on second floor without lift) and personal factors (age 62, retired teacher).
  • An ICF-written problem list converts directly into SMART goals that can be retested at discharge.
  • Evidence-based practice: the history sets the pretest probability. Sackett's model says a test result means something only when it moves probability away from what the history already told us — a positive test in a low-probability patient is often a false positive.
  • Conclusion: history taking is the first and highest-yield assessment, not paperwork before assessment — a physiotherapist who listens well needs fewer machines, not more.
  • Four-step flow: 1. LISTEN (chief complaint + OPQRST) → 2. SCREEN (red flags / yellow flags) → 3. HYPOTHESISE (2 to 3 working diagnoses, written down before touching the patient) → 4. TEST (focused objective assessment + outcome measures, then set ICF goals).

Examiner's tip: open with "the subjective examination generates hypotheses; the objective examination tests them" — that sentence plus a named red-flag list separates a 6/10 script from a 9/10 script.

Sources
  • Sackett DL, Straus SE, Richardson WS, et al. Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM.
  • Herbert RD, Jamtvedt G, Mead J, Hagen KB. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
  • World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice and Ethical Principles.
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
210 marks

Q2. Instrumentation techniques — discuss the instrumentation of therapeutic and electrophysiological devices used in physiotherapy practice (generators, stimulators, EMG and nerve conduction equipment, waveforms and safety).

Full answer →

Explain the instrumentation chain for therapeutic stimulators and for EMG/NCS equipment, the controls and waveforms, and electrical safety.

  • What earns marks: the instrumentation chain concept and its stages (2 marks) · therapeutic stimulators — circuit blocks, controls, waveforms (2.5 marks) · electrophysiological equipment — EMG and NCS instrumentation (2.5 marks) · electrical safety — leakage, earthing, isolation, standards (2 marks); calibration and conclusion (1 mark).
  • The instrumentation chain: every device, therapeutic or diagnostic, is a chain — a source or sensor, a stage that shapes or amplifies the signal, a processing stage, and an output or display.
  • A therapeutic stimulator carries energy from the mains to the patient as a controlled waveform; a diagnostic machine carries a tiny biological signal from the patient to a display. Once you can draw the chain, every machine is just a variation on it.
  • Therapeutic stimulator block sequence: mains input → power supply (step-down, rectification, smoothing) → oscillator and timer → pulse-shaping circuit → output amplifier → isolation transformer → patient via electrodes.
  • Frequency (pulses per second): 50 to 100 Hz for conventional sensory TENS, 2 to 4 Hz for acupuncture-like TENS, 30 to 50 Hz for tetanic muscle contraction.
  • Pulse duration in microseconds: short pulses around 50 to 200 µs favour sensory nerves; longer 200 to 400 µs pulses recruit motor axons; millisecond-to-hundred-millisecond pulses are needed for denervated muscle.
  • Amplitude is set in milliamperes, and ramp or surge makes the contraction comfortable.
  • Modern units deliver charge-balanced biphasic pulsed waveforms (symmetrical or asymmetrical) so no net DC passes through skin and electrolytic burns are avoided; classical faradic and interrupted direct currents belong to the older monophasic generation.
  • EMG/NCS — here the patient is the source. Recording or stimulating electrodes feed a differential amplifier, which subtracts the signal on one electrode from the other so the noise common to both (chiefly 50 Hz mains interference in India) cancels.
  • The quality of that cancellation is the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), and a good EMG amplifier has a very high one.
  • Band-pass filters (roughly 10 Hz to 10 kHz for needle EMG) remove drift and high-frequency hash.
  • The signal then goes to a loudspeaker (the experienced ear grades a motor unit before the eye does), a display with adjustable gain in microvolts or millivolts per division, and a trigger-and-delay line for motor unit analysis.
  • For nerve conduction studies a separate stimulator delivers supramaximal pulses while latency, amplitude and conduction velocity are computed; sensory and mixed responses are so small that signal averaging of repeated sweeps is used.
  • Calibration: sweep speed and gain must be checked against the machine's own calibrator before relying on numbers.
  • Safety — distinguish macroshock (current through intact skin, painful, burns) from microshock (current reaching the heart directly through a central line or pacing wire, where tiny currents can precipitate fibrillation).
  • Protection comes from good earthing, isolation transformers so the patient circuit floats, current-limiting output stages, and enclosure integrity.
  • International standards (IEC 60601 family) classify applied parts — Type B and BF limited to about 100 microamperes patient leakage, Type CF (cardiac floating) to about 10 microamperes.
  • Indian ground realities: voltage fluctuation demands a stabiliser, damp monsoon walls destroy earthing, and the annual biomedical calibration visit is the first line of defence.
  • Application and conclusion: a clinician who understands instrumentation chooses parameters by mechanism rather than a protocol card, recognises a faulty machine (drifting output, cracked leads, corroded electrodes), and documents device settings like a prescription — it is dose control for electrotherapy and signal fidelity for diagnosis.

Examiner's tip: write the word "isolation" in the stimulator chain and "CMRR" in the EMG chain — these two words alone signal instrumentation literacy.

Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA, et al. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
310 marks

Q3. Musculoskeletal adaptations to exercise and training.

Full answer →

Show the order of adaptation (neural first, then muscle, then matrix) and apply it to exercise prescription and detraining.

  • What earns marks: neural adaptations — the early gains (2 marks) · muscular adaptations — hypertrophy and fibre phenotype (2.5 marks) · tendon, ligament, bone and cartilage adaptations (2 marks) · metabolic and cardiorespiratory support with Indian context (2 marks); application to prescription and detraining (1.5 marks).
  • Adaptation follows a fixed order: skill, then drive, then tissue.
  • In the first weeks of a strength programme nearly all the force gain is neural — improved motor unit recruitment, higher firing rates (rate coding), better synchronisation, and reduced antagonist co-activation (first 2 to 8 weeks).
  • That is why beginners double their performance in a month while arm circumference barely changes, and why these same weeks are when physiotherapy re-education works — the window for motor relearning opens fastest here.
  • Muscle — hypertrophy: with continued loading, myofibrillar hypertrophy dominates. Contractile protein synthesis outstrips breakdown, actin and myosin are added, and the fibre grows in cross-section — fastest in type II fibres.
  • Muscle shifts along its phenotypic spectrum rather than swapping fibre classes: type IIx myosin heavy chain expression falls toward IIa with almost any regular training, giving a more oxidative, fatigue-resistant profile. True hyperplasia (fibre splitting) is minor and debated in humans.
  • Endurance-type training instead adds capillaries per fibre and mitochondrial density — so the response is decided by the dose: heavy few-rep loading builds protein, long low-load work builds oxidative machinery.
  • Tendon and ligament: collagenous tissues adapt slower and later. Tendon stiffness rises with heavy loading over months, driven by collagen synthesis that peaks well after the exercise bout.
  • Bone follows Wolff's law — it thickens along lines of mechanical strain, so impact and heavy weight-bearing build bone density site-specifically (the femoral neck of a loader, the forearm of a racket player), while bed rest and immobilisation resorb it.
  • Cartilage: articular cartilage has no blood supply in adult life and depends on cyclic compression for nutrition — moderate, regular joint loading is cartilage food, whereas sustained static loading starves it.
  • Ligaments regain tensile strength slowly after injury — which is why a sprained ligament needs months of graded loading, not weeks.
  • Metabolic support: training raises glycogen storage capacity, enzyme activity in the energy pathways, glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity — muscle becomes a bigger glucose sink, the basis for prescribing resistance and aerobic work for diabetes and metabolic syndrome.
  • Indian context: the Misra JAPI 2009 consensus documented that Asian Indians carry more body fat and abdominal adiposity at any BMI, with metabolic syndrome arriving earlier, so it recommended daily physical activity including muscle-strengthening exercise as treatment, not recreation.
  • Support systems adapt in parallel — blood volume, stroke volume and capillary density rise, and acid-buffering capacity improves, so the trained muscle recovers between sets.
  • Prescribe by adaptation, not habit: neural re-education needs motor-control work in the early phase; hypertrophy needs 60 to 70 per cent of one repetition maximum across 8 to 12 repetitions; tendon and bone need months of progressive loading — which is why tendinopathy programmes run 12 weeks, not 2.
  • Detraining unwinds the stack in reverse and faster: neural drive and capillarisation decay within weeks of stopping, hypertrophy regresses more slowly, and bone mass takes longest both to build and to lose.
  • Timeline conclusion: neural first (weeks 2 to 8), hypertrophy second (8+), matrix last (months) — the same exercise, different tissue answering, depending on how long it has been going on.

Examiner's tip: quote the sequence "neural first, hypertrophy second, matrix last" and anchor each phase to a clinical example (early quadriceps re-education, a 12-week gym phase, a long tendon-loading programme).

Sources
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Misra A, Chowbey P, Makkar BM, et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. J Assoc Physicians India 2009;57:163-70.
410 marks

Q4. Muscle plasticity in response to electrical stimulation.

Full answer →

Define muscle plasticity, explain how electrical stimulation recruits and remodels muscle, give the parameters that drive it, and its clinical uses.

  • What earns marks: concept and definition of muscle plasticity (1.5 marks) · mechanism — recruitment pattern and fibre transformation with chronic stimulation (3 marks) · stimulation parameters that drive the plastic response (2.5 marks) · clinical applications with examples (2 marks); limitations and conclusion (1 mark).
  • Plasticity is the ability of muscle to remodel its structure and function to match the demands placed on it — the use-it-or-lose-it principle written in protein.
  • Voluntary demand sculpts muscle through the nervous system; electrical stimulation sculpts it by depolarising the motor axons directly, bypassing the central nervous system entirely.
  • That bypass is both the power and the limitation of the method — it forces muscle to contract in a way the body would never voluntarily choose.
  • Voluntary recruitment follows Henneman's size principle — small, fatigue-resistant motor units first, large fast units only as force demands rise, asynchronously and spread across the muscle.
  • Electrical stimulation inverts this: current density is highest beneath the electrodes, and large-diameter axons have lower thresholds, so it recruits motor units in reverse — non-selectively, spatially fixed near the electrodes, and all synchronously in every pulse.
  • So the stimulated contraction fatigues faster than a voluntary contraction of equal force.
  • The classic demonstration of true plasticity is chronic low-frequency stimulation (Salmons and Vrbova, 1969): fast, fatigable muscle stimulated continuously at around 10 to 20 Hz for weeks transforms into a slow, oxidative, fatigue-resistant muscle — myosin heavy-chain isoforms switch, oxidative enzymes rise, capillary supply improves.
  • The muscle reads the input pattern, not the cause of it, and rebuilds itself accordingly. At the other pole, silence is also a signal: immobilisation and denervation strip protein rapidly, which stimulation can partially offset.
  • Parameters — frequency: 30 to 50 Hz produces tetanic contraction for strengthening, while long programmes at low frequency bias the muscle toward endurance characteristics.
  • Pulse duration: 200 to 400 µs favours motor axon recruitment; denervated muscle needs pulses in the millisecond range, since the muscle membrane itself must now be excited.
  • Amplitude: strong but comfortable contraction, ramped to tolerance.
  • Duty cycle: roughly 1:5 on-to-off for strengthening, because stimulated muscle fatigues early.
  • Duration and schedule: 10 to 20 contractions per session, several sessions weekly, over weeks for remodelling. Electrode placement over the motor point of the target muscle buys maximum contraction for minimum current.
  • Clinical uses: preventing disuse atrophy in immobilised limbs (post-plaster quadriceps, bed-rest patients); re-educating inhibited muscle after surgery or effusion (the post-arthroscopy quadriceps that will not switch on voluntarily); strengthening when volitional control is poor or pain limits effort; maintaining trophic status in orthopaedic and some neurological cases; and stimulating denervated muscle with long-duration pulses to slow protein loss until reinnervation.
  • Limitations: stimulation is uncomfortable, fatigues the muscle quickly, and its strength gains transfer best when combined with voluntary effort — it is an adjuvant to exercise, never a replacement.
  • Conclusion: electrical stimulation is a controlled message to muscle plasticity, and the message content — frequency, duration, duty cycle, weeks of exposure — decides whether the muscle hears "be strong", "be enduring" or merely "do not disappear".

Examiner's tip: the trio "non-selective, spatially fixed, temporally synchronous" describes stimulated recruitment — memorise it, then immediately contrast it with the size principle.

Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Salmons S, Vrbova G. The influence of activity on some contractile characteristics of mammalian fast and slow muscles. J Physiol 1969;201:535-49.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA, et al. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
510 marks

Q5. Define probability and normal distribution.

Full answer →

Define probability and the normal distribution, state their rules and properties, and give the empirical rule and the standard normal (Z) variable.

  • What earns marks: probability — definition and the three approaches (2.5 marks) · axioms and rules — addition, multiplication, conditional (1.5 marks) · normal distribution — definition and properties (2.5 marks) · empirical rule and the standard normal (Z) variable (2 marks); applications in physiotherapy research and practice (1.5 marks).
  • Probability is a number between 0 and 1 (equivalently 0 to 100 per cent) that quantifies the chance that an event occurs; 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, and every real-world event lives strictly in between.
  • Classical (a priori) probability applies when outcomes are equally likely: probability equals favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes — the chance of a coin landing heads is one in two, with no experiment required.
  • Empirical (frequentist) probability is the limit of the relative frequency in a long series of trials: if 60 of our last 200 frozen-shoulder patients recovered full abduction within 12 weeks, our best estimate of that event is 0.3.
  • Subjective probability is a degree of belief — the clinician's gut number before data arrive, honest enough to be labelled as such.
  • Kolmogorov's axioms: probability of any event lies between 0 and 1; probability of the certain event (the whole sample space) is 1; and mutually exclusive events add.
  • Addition rule: probability of A or B equals probability of A plus probability of B minus probability of A and B. For independent events the multiplication rule: probability of A and B equals the product.
  • Conditional probability (probability of A given B) is the doorway to Bayes' theorem — how a test result should update our belief about the patient in front of us.
  • The normal (Gaussian) distribution is a continuous probability distribution for a variable that results from the sum of many small independent influences; its density curve is the symmetric, bell-shaped curve.
  • It is defined entirely by two parameters — the mean (µ), which fixes its centre, and the standard deviation (σ), which fixes its spread.
  • Properties: it is unimodal and symmetric, so mean equals median equals mode.
  • Total area under the curve is 1, so areas are probabilities.
  • The curve is asymptotic — the tails approach but never touch the axis.
  • Points of inflection lie one σ either side of the mean; and there is a family of curves, one for each µ-σ pair.
  • Empirical rule: for any normal distribution, roughly 68.27 per cent of values lie within one σ of the mean, 95.44 per cent within two σ, and 99.73 per cent within three σ.
  • Standard normal: Z equals X minus µ divided by σ maps any normal variable onto the standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, whose areas are tabulated — this one transformation lets us compare a patient's haemoglobin, a class's exam score and a study's sample mean on a single scale.
  • Why a physiotherapist cares: normal distributions generate laboratory reference ranges (the central 95 per cent), underpin quality-control flagging of outlier results, and form the sampling distribution of the mean that the central limit theorem guarantees — the licence for the t-test and ANOVA.
  • Conclusion: probability is the grammar, the normal curve is the commonest sentence, and parametric statistics is a conversation conducted almost entirely in that sentence.

Examiner's tip: keep probability "between 0 and 1" and normal "defined by two parameters, µ and σ" stated crisply, then give one numeric example (a laboratory range) to prove you can use it.

Sources
  • Indrayan A. Medical Biostatistics.
  • Hulley SB, Cummings SR, Browner WS, et al. Designing Clinical Research.
610 marks

Q6. Instrumentation of NMES (neuromuscular electrical stimulation).

Full answer →

Draw the NMES block diagram and explain each stage, give the controls and waveform, the safety features and contraindications, and one worked dose.

  • What earns marks: block diagram of an NMES unit with the function of each stage (3 marks) · controls and waveforms — the clinically adjustable parameters (2.5 marks) · output circuit, electrodes and patient factors (1.5 marks) · safety features and contraindications (2 marks); calibration and a worked clinical setting (1 mark).
  • NMES is the use of a pulsed electrical current to evoke a visible muscle contraction through its motor nerve — as distinct from TENS, which aims at sensory nerves.
  • The instrument, whatever the brand, is one chain: mains through a power supply (step-down transformer, rectification, smoothing) → an oscillator and master timer that set pulse rate and treatment time → a pulse-shaping circuit that fixes pulse duration and waveform → an output amplifier delivering current at the set amplitude with a ramp generator shaping the rise time → an isolation transformer separating the patient circuit from the mains, so no fault can pass wall power to the patient.
  • Modern clinical units make the ramp an explicit knob, because comfort (and therefore treatment tolerance) lives at the leading edge of the pulse train.
  • Frequency: 30 to 50 Hz for tetanic strengthening contractions; lower rates suit sensory and endurance goals.
  • Pulse duration: 200 to 400 µs to preferentially depolarise motor axons.
  • Amplitude: raised slowly to a strong but tolerable contraction. Units operate close to constant-current behaviour, so the machine pushes the voltage needed to keep the programmed milliamperes flowing as skin impedance changes — which is why amplitude, not voltage, is the honest measure of dose.
  • Waveform: charge-balanced biphasic rectangular pulses, so each cathodic phase is cancelled by an anodic one and no net direct current chemically burns the skin; classic Russian current is a 2.5 kHz carrier delivered in bursts at 50 per second.
  • Rhythm/duty cycle: alternates contraction and rest (about 10 seconds on to 50 seconds off for strengthening), because stimulated muscle — recruited in reverse order — fatigues earlier than voluntary muscle.
  • Patient circuit: self-adhesive hydrogel electrodes sized to the target muscle; the active electrode over the motor point for the strongest contraction at the least current.
  • Inter-electrode distance shapes the current path; skin must be clean and intact, and poor contact concentrates current density into a burn.
  • Impedance varies with sweating, oedema and electrode age — a session started comfortably in a sweating patient can drift uncomfortable within minutes, so check back, do not set and walk away.
  • Hardware safety: isolation of the patient circuit, current-limited output, charge balance, timer cutoff, and periodic calibration against a test load in the biomedical department.
  • Contraindications: demand pacemakers and implanted electronic devices, the abdomen during pregnancy, active malignancy in the region, deep vein thrombosis in the limb (risk of embolus), and over anaesthetic or absent skin sensation.
  • Never place electrodes so current crosses the heart, and never assume a ward machine is calibrated because its display lights up.
  • Worked setting for quadriceps strengthening after knee immobilisation: biphasic pulses, 300 µs, 45 Hz, ramp 2 seconds, 10 seconds on with 50 seconds off, 12 to 15 contractions, three sessions weekly for 4 to 6 weeks, amplitude to strong visible contraction — documented in the record exactly like a drug prescription.
  • Conclusion: the instrument exists to deliver a reproducible dose; the therapist who understands each block knows exactly which knob changes which physiological outcome.

Examiner's tip: don't just list knob names — map each knob to physiology (frequency to tetany, pulse duration to axon selectivity, duty cycle to fatigue protection). One sentence per knob.

Sources
  • Kisner C, Colby LA, et al. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
710 marks

Q7. Testing of hypothesis (null and alternative hypotheses, type I and type II errors, p-value, steps, one-tailed and two-tailed tests).

Full answer →

Define the hypotheses, give the five steps, contrast one-tailed and two-tailed tests, and explain type I/II errors, power and the p-value.

  • What earns marks: hypotheses defined and the five steps of testing (2.5 marks) · one-tailed versus two-tailed tests with examples (1.5 marks) · type I and type II errors, significance level, power (3 marks) · p-value — meaning, decision rule, common misconceptions (2 marks); application to a physiotherapy study and conclusion (1 mark).
  • A hypothesis is a testable statement about a population parameter.
  • The null hypothesis (H0) asserts no difference or no association (the new mobilisation technique is no better than standard care); the alternative hypothesis (H1) asserts that a difference or association exists. Because we can never prove anything with a sample, we try to reject the null.
  • Five steps: 1) state H0 and H1; 2) choose the significance level α (conventionally 0.05); 3) select the right test for the data type and design (paired t-test, independent t-test, chi-square, ANOVA); 4) compute the test statistic and its p-value; 5) decide — reject H0 if the p-value is less than or equal to α, otherwise fail to reject it.
  • Wording matters: we never "accept" H0, we only fail to reject it — absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
  • Two-tailed test: looks for a difference in either direction and splits α across both tails — use it unless a difference in one direction is meaningless or impossible.
  • One-tailed test: places all of α in a single tail; justified only when the alternative hypothesis was directional before the data were seen (e.g. our new protocol is claimed to reduce pain score).
  • Ethics: choosing one tail after seeing the trend is not statistics, it is story-telling, and it inflates the apparent significance.
  • Type I error: rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true — a false positive, the "fooling yourself" error; its probability is α, the significance level we set.
  • Type II error: failing to reject a null that is false — a false negative; its probability is β.
  • Power equals 1 minus β — the chance of detecting a real difference — and is conventionally targeted at 80 per cent or more.
  • Levers: increasing sample size and effect size raises power, and reducing measurement noise tightens it; α and β trade off against each other for a fixed sample size — which is why the α of 0.05 is a social contract, not a law of nature.
  • Underpowered pilot studies reported as negative are the commonest type II error habitat in student theses.
  • The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
  • Small p means "such data would be surprising if the null held" — which is evidence against the null, nothing more.
  • What it is not: not the probability that the null is true, not the probability the result is due to chance in general, and p of 0.04 versus 0.06 is not a cliff edge.
  • Report it with the confidence interval, which shows the size and uncertainty of the effect — the question the clinician actually needs answered.
  • Worked example: does six weeks of mobilisation plus exercise beat exercise alone for frozen shoulder? H0: no difference in SPADI change scores; H1: a difference exists (two-tailed); α 0.05; independent t-test on change scores; suppose p equals 0.03 with a mean difference of 9 points on the 0-100 scale — we reject H0, then immediately ask whether 9 points clears the minimal clinically important difference.
  • Conclusion: hypothesis testing is a filter for chance, not a verdict on usefulness — the number that matters after the p-value is whether the patient can feel the difference.

Examiner's tip: the single most-rewarded sentence is the definition of p — "the probability of data this extreme or more if the null is true" — followed by the misconception (p is not the probability that the null is true).

Sources
  • Indrayan A. Medical Biostatistics.
  • Hulley SB, Cummings SR, Browner WS, et al. Designing Clinical Research.
810 marks

Q8. Discuss the psychometric properties of SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index).

Full answer →

Describe SPADI's structure and scoring, then its reliability, validity and responsiveness, quoting the key numbers.

  • What earns marks: description, structure and scoring of SPADI (2.5 marks) · reliability — internal consistency, test-retest, measurement error (2.5 marks) · validity — construct, convergent, criterion (2.5 marks) · responsiveness — MCID and MDC (1.5 marks); Indian language versions and clinical use (1 mark).
  • Psychometric properties are what make a patient-reported outcome measure's measurements trustworthy.
  • SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index), developed by Roach and colleagues in 1991, is a self-administered, region-specific shoulder scale of 13 items in two subscales.
  • Pain subscale — 5 items: pain at its worst, lying on the involved side, reaching to a high shelf, touching the back of the neck, pushing with the involved arm.
  • Disability subscale — 8 items: washing hair, washing the back, pulling on a sweater, buttoning a shirt, putting on pants, placing an object on a high shelf, carrying a 10-pound object, removing something from the back pocket.
  • Scoring: each item is scored on an 11-point numerical rating scale from 0 to 10; the total (out of 130) is expressed as a percentage — 0 meaning a perfect shoulder and 100 the worst imaginable.
  • It suits busy Indian OPDs because it takes two to three minutes.
  • Internal consistency is high: Cronbach's alpha has ranged from about 0.86 to 0.96 across studies — above the 0.7 floor and below the 0.95 zone where items merely repeat each other.
  • Test-retest reliability is likewise high in later studies — intra-class correlation coefficients commonly between about 0.84 and 0.95 for the total score (the original 1991 development sample reported more modest values around 0.64).
  • Measurement error must be quoted alongside: on the 0-100 scale, the minimal detectable change (MDC95) is about 18 points, so a repeated-measurement difference smaller than that is indistinguishable from noise.
  • Construct validity: factor analysis supports the two-factor (pain and disability) structure, though some studies find a single dominant factor — worth one honest line in an exam answer.
  • Convergent validity: SPADI correlates strongly with other upper-limb measures such as the DASH (correlations around 0.7 to 0.9 across validation studies) and moderately with pain ratings and generic measures like SF-36 physical scores, as expected for a region-specific tool.
  • Criterion validity is the soft spot — there is no universally accepted gold standard for shoulder disability, so SPADI anchors itself against ROM and clinical change; in the original study it correlated negatively with shoulder range of motion, and it detects change in clinical status over short intervals.
  • Responsiveness: SPADI is responsive in conditions from adhesive capsulitis to post-arthroplasty follow-up.
  • MCID — the smallest change a patient would actually notice — has been estimated at roughly 8 to 13 points on the 0-100 scale across studies (8, 10 and about 13 have all been reported), with values near the higher end after procedures such as arthroplasty.
  • Read the numbers together: statistical significance decides whether the treatment beat noise; crossing the MCID decides whether the patient cares; and change below the MDC cannot be claimed as change at all.
  • Indian versions: the Hindi SPADI (translated per AAOS guidelines; in overhead athletes with impingement, internal consistency about 0.75, test-retest ICC about 0.87, convergent correlation 0.94 with Hindi DASH, MDC95 about 14) and a Tamil version validated in Hong Kong Physiotherapy Journal, 2012.
  • Conclusion: SPADI is a short, reliable, valid and responsive shoulder-specific measure whose numbers are only interpretable through its psychometric properties — the same 9-point improvement can be noise in one context and a patient-felt success in another.

Examiner's tip: never quote a reliability number without naming its statistic, and never quote MCID without MDC — the pair shows you understand measurement error.

Sources
  • Roach KE, Budiman-Mak E, Songsiridej N, Lertratanakul Y. Development of a shoulder pain and disability index. Arthritis Care Res 1991;4:143-9.
  • Jeldi AJ, Aseer AL, Dhandapani AG, Roach KE. Cross-cultural adaptation, reliability and validity of an Indian (Tamil) version for the SPADI. Hong Kong Physiother J 2012;30:99-104.
  • Sharma N, Sharma S, Kataria C. Translation and adaptation of SPADI into Hindi. Indian J Physiother Occup Ther 2011;5(4):142-5.
  • Herbert RD, Jamtvedt G, Mead J, Hagen KB. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
910 marks

Q9. Bloom's Taxonomy.

Full answer →

Give the 1956 and revised 2001 taxonomies, the other two domains, and apply the taxonomy to writing intended learning outcomes and assessments.

  • What earns marks: original 1956 taxonomy — the six cognitive levels (2.5 marks) · revised 2001 taxonomy and the knowledge dimension (2.5 marks) · affective and psychomotor domains (1.5 marks) · application — writing ILOs and assessments (2.5 marks); conclusion — link to Miller's pyramid (1 mark).
  • A taxonomy is a classification that orders things by complexity; Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives (Bloom and colleagues, 1956) orders cognitive learning outcomes from simple recall to the highest forms of thinking.
  • The original six levels, each requiring those below it: knowledge (recall facts — name the ulnar nerve roots), comprehension (explain in your own words), application (use the rule in a new patient), analysis (break a gait pattern into its deviations), synthesis (assemble a treatment plan), and evaluation (judge which plan is best, and defend the choice).
  • Two claims matter for teaching: the hierarchy is cumulative (a student cannot analyze what they do not understand), and it pushes teachers to aim above the recall level where most exams quietly live.
  • Revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001): the levels were renamed as verbs and the top two swapped — remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create — with creation now at the apex.
  • Its deeper change is that it is two-dimensional: the cognitive process dimension is crossed with a knowledge dimension of four types of content.
  • The four knowledge types: factual (terminology, details), conceptual (classifications, principles), procedural (techniques, methods), and metacognitive (knowledge of one's own thinking, and of oneself as a learner).
  • A learning outcome is therefore a cell in a grid: "design (create) a graded eccentric loading programme (procedural)" is a different cell from "list the contraindications (factual, remember)"; postgraduate physiotherapy training lives almost entirely in the higher cells.
  • Affective domain (Krathwohl's hierarchy: receiving, responding, valuing, organizing, characterizing) tracks how attitudes form — the student who first attends to patient counselling, then practises it, then values it, until professional empathy is character.
  • Psychomotor domain (Simpson's and Harrow's versions: perception, set, guided response, mechanism, complex overt response) is where manual skills progress from clumsy imitation to automatic mastery — the physiotherapist's home domain.
  • A complete lesson plan touches all three domains: the student must know, must care, and must do.
  • Application: intended learning outcomes should be written with observable verbs at the intended level — "list" and "define" sit at remember; "differentiate" at analyze; "construct" or "justify" at create and evaluate.
  • Verbs like "know", "understand" and "appreciate" are unmarkable because nobody can observe them.
  • Assessment must align with the outcome (constructive alignment): an ILO promising analysis cannot be tested by a recall MCQ, and a viva that only asks "define TENS" has silently lowered the level of the whole course.
  • Use the grid as a checklist when preparing a class: name the cell you are aiming at before writing the slide.
  • Conclusion — Bloom meets Miller: Bloom's cognitive domain pairs naturally with Miller's pyramid of assessment — knows (the base, Bloom's remember), knows how (apply and analyze), shows how (psychomotor domain under observation) and does (performance in real practice).
  • Bloom's taxonomy is the operating system of physiotherapy education — it decides what we ask in vivas, what our MCQs actually test, and whether we are training recallers of electrotherapy lists or clinicians who can create and defend a treatment decision.

Examiner's tip: quote one physiotherapy-specific verb pair at each level (define SPADI at remember, justify the treatment plan at evaluate) — examiners reward using the taxonomy, not reciting its ladder.

Sources
  • Anderson LW, Krathwohl LH, et al. A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives. New York: Longman; 2001.
  • Bloom BS, et al. Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, Handbook I: The Cognitive Domain. New York: David McKay; 1956.
  • Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Acad Med 1990;65:S63-7.
1010 marks

Q10. Describe the different methods used in strength training.

Full answer →

Describe the strength-training methods (isometric, isotonic, isokinetic, plyometric), the dosage, the special regimes, and match each method to a patient.

  • What earns marks: isometric and isotonic (concentric and eccentric) methods (2.5 marks) · isokinetic and plyometric methods (2.5 marks) · dosage — intensity, sets, repetitions, frequency, progression (2.5 marks) · special regimes — variable resistance, circuit training, periodisation (1.5 marks); clinical application and Indian context, conclusion (1 mark).
  • Classify methods by what happens to muscle length and joint angle.
  • Isometric: the muscle develops tension without changing length — the joint does not move. The strength gain is angle-specific (plus a small spill-over of roughly 10 to 20 degrees either side), so several angles must be trained.
  • Isometric is the method of choice when movement is prohibited or painful — post-operative limbs, painful arthritic joints, and a patient in a cast; brief maximal holds, for example a six-second contraction repeated several times at multiple angles.
  • Isotonic (dynamic): the joint moves — the concentric phase shortens the muscle to lift, the eccentric phase lengthens it under load to lower.
  • Eccentric loading produces greater force per unit of activation and a better hypertrophy stimulus, at the price of delayed-onset muscle soreness — which is why it is both the tool of choice in tendinopathy rehabilitation (heavy slow resistance, eccentric decline protocols) and something to grade carefully in the untrained.
  • Isokinetic training keeps limb velocity constant while the machine accommodates resistance moment to moment, so the muscle works maximally through the whole range — free weights are hardest only where leverage is worst.
  • Computerised dynamometers (Cybex, Biodex) also quantify torque, making this the reference standard for strength testing as well as a training mode, across a spectrum of angular velocities.
  • Plyometric training works the stretch-shortening cycle: a rapid eccentric pre-load stores elastic energy, and the immediate concentric recoil spends it — depth jumps, bounding, medicine-ball throws.
  • Plyometrics train power rather than pure strength, demand a strength base and sound landing mechanics first, and belong to late-stage athletic rehabilitation.
  • Dosage — intensity: a novice begins around 60 to 70 per cent of one repetition maximum; advanced lifters train at 80 per cent and above.
  • Volume: about 8 to 12 repetitions per set for general strengthening (heavier loads and fewer repetitions for pure strength; lighter loads to muscular failure for hypertrophy), typically 2 to 4 sets per muscle group.
  • Rest: 2 to 3 minutes between sets for strength work. Frequency: 2 to 3 sessions per week per muscle group, because the muscle grows between sessions, not during them.
  • Every plan runs on progressive overload — small systematic increases in load, volume or frequency as adaptation allows — paired with the principle of specificity: you get precisely what you train.
  • Variable-resistance equipment (cam-and-lever machines) varies resistance to match the natural strength curve through the range.
  • Circuit resistance training strings stations together with short rests for combined strength and conditioning in limited time.
  • Bodyweight and elastic-resistance training deliver progressive overload without a gym — the practical backbone of Indian home programmes.
  • Periodisation structures training into phases (hypertrophy, strength, power, deload) so peak performance arrives at the right competition or season; the same logic phases a rehabilitation programme from control, to capacity, to power.
  • Clinical matching: post-operative knee — isometric quadriceps setting progressing to eccentric work; anterior knee pain — closed-chain weight-bearing work; older adults — power training (the ability to react quickly fades faster than strength and predicts falls); metabolic risk — the Misra JAPI 2009 consensus for Asian Indians prescribes muscle-strengthening activity on most days as part of daily physical activity, not an optional extra.
  • Conclusion: there is no best method — there is a best match between method, stage of healing, and goal, held together by measurable dosage and progressive overload.

Examiner's tip: end each method's paragraph with "so it is used when..." — a method without a clinical indication is trivia; a method matched to a patient phase is prescription.

Sources
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA, et al. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  • Misra A, Chowbey P, Makkar BM, et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. J Assoc Physicians India 2009;57:163-70.
110 marks

Describe the documentation procedure adopted in terms of assessment, management in rehabilitation based on International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF).

Full answer →

Explain the ICF model, then show how you document assessment findings and rehabilitation plans using ICF codes and qualifiers.

  • What earns marks: cover all four rows of the marking scheme — define ICF and its purpose (WHO 2001), draw the components, show assessment codes, then show management planning.
  • Never call ICF a "classification of disability" — the C stands for functioning AND disability, and forgetting environmental factors is the commonest way to lose the full two marks of the components row.
  • What ICF is: the World Health Organization's working form of the biopsychosocial model. Instead of documenting only the disease (ICD), we document what the disease does to the person.
  • Functioning and disability are the health condition interacting with body functions, body structures, activities, participation, and the surrounding environmental and personal factors.
  • The shift examiners look for: from "what is wrong with the knee" to "what the stiff knee does to the farmer who has to squat to work."
  • ICF has two parts. Part 1 covers functioning and disability with three components: body functions (code b), body structures (code s), and activities and participation (code d).
  • Part 2 covers contextual factors: environmental factors (code e) and personal factors, which are described but not classified.
  • Every code carries a qualifier from 0 to 4 — no impairment to complete impairment. So d450.2 means moderate difficulty walking.
  • Fig to draw: health condition on top, the three functioning boxes in the middle, contextual factors at the bottom; every arrow is two-way — each box can help or harm the others.
  • Assessment procedure (post-stroke patient, district hospital OPD): organise history and examination findings by level.
  • Body function and structure: b730 muscle power impairment 2, spasticity b735.1, shoulder subluxation s73016.
  • Activity: d450 walking with quadripod, moderate limitation.
  • Participation: d920 recreation and d850 remunerative employment, severely restricted.
  • Contextual factors: e310 immediate family is supportive (facilitator, +3); e140 work products absent; e115 assistive products unavailable in the village (barrier).
  • Each finding gets a code plus a qualifier — that pairing is what turns a case sheet into ICF documentation.
  • Management documentation: write SMART goals at each level.
  • Body level goal: improve shoulder abduction power by one MRC grade in six weeks.
  • Activity goal: independent walking for 200 metres with a stick by week eight.
  • Participation goal: return to light farm work by twelve weeks.
  • Every intervention column must cite the level it targets, and every re-assessment must use the same qualifiers so the change is measurable.
  • Link standard scales to codes: the SPADI documents shoulder pain and disability; a 10-metre walk test documents d450.
  • Why examiners award this: ICF prevents impairment-only physiotherapy, gives the whole rehabilitation team a common language, and justifies goal setting the family understands.
  • Indian context: it forces you to document environmental barriers — a house with a squat toilet, a workplace with no seating, a bus with a high step — which decides whether your exercise programme translates to real life.
Sources
  • World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice.
  • WHO. International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), 2001.
  • Roach KE et al. The Shoulder Pain and Disability Index. Arthritis Care & Research, 1991.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
210 marks

Define Competency. Add a note on Competency-Based Physiotherapy Education.

Full answer →

Define competency with all three domains, then explain how competency-based physiotherapy education designs teaching and assessment around outcomes.

  • What earns marks: the definition must contain all three domains AND the word "habitual".
  • Link CBPE to assessment at the apex of Miller's pyramid ("does").
  • Use Bloom's taxonomy verbs (assess, evaluate, create) instead of "understand" to pick up easy extra marks.
  • Definition: competency is the habitual and judicious integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes displayed in real clinical practice.
  • Three domains, never two — knowledge, skills, attitudes. A therapist who passes a written test on gait training but cannot communicate the plan to an anxious grandfather is knowledgeable, not competent.
  • "Habitual" matters: one lucky performance on exam day is not competency; it must be reproducible over time and across situations.
  • CBPE turns the curriculum inside-out: instead of "we taught ten lectures on electrotherapy, therefore the student is ready," it declares the desired graduate outcome first (the competent entry-level clinician) and designs teaching, learning and assessment backwards from it. This is constructive alignment.
  • Content is organised into competencies with milestones that state observable behaviours, mapped to Bloom's revised taxonomy verbs — a student must be able to assess, plan, apply and evaluate, not merely describe.
  • Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) convert competencies into real clinical units of work, such as "assess and manage a patient with mechanical low back pain under supervision."
  • Assessment — George Miller's pyramid: base "knows" (MCQs), "knows how" (case discussions and vivas), "shows how" (OSCE stations on simulated patients), apex "does" (workplace-based assessment and direct observation at the patient's side).
  • In CBPE the dominant assessment becomes the apex; feedback is continuous and formative rather than a single summative verdict; progression is by demonstrated achievement, not time served.
  • Advantages: transparency of outcomes, learner-centred flexibility (a student may take twelve weeks or sixteen to master a skill), early clinical exposure, and assessment that mirrors actual practice.
  • Challenges in India: batch sizes of sixty-plus make individualised feedback expensive; faculty need training in direct observation; workplace assessment demands clinical infrastructure that colleges attached to small hospitals struggle to provide; and a national competency framework for physiotherapy is still maturing, though the CBME model adopted for MBBS gives a ready template.
Sources
  • Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Academic Medicine, 1990.
  • Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing (Bloom revised).
  • World Physiotherapy. Physiotherapist education framework and Standards of Practice.
310 marks

Describe various methods of sampling and sample size determination.

Full answer →

List the sampling methods with examples, then give the sample-size formula and the worked figure.

  • What earns marks: define population, sample and sampling frame first; then list probability and non-probability methods with examples; then give the sample-size formula with the worked figure of 384.
  • Always write "sample size was calculated for the primary outcome" — a study powered for one outcome is not powered for all of them.
  • Why we sample: studying the entire population of Indian knee-osteoarthritis patients is impossible, but the sample must behave like the population it came from.
  • Three terms: target population (everyone we want to study), accessible population (those we can reach), and sampling frame — the complete, reachable list of population members from which you actually draw.
  • In India the frame is the honest weak link: electoral rolls miss migrants, hospital registers miss those who never reach hospital — every such gap is selection bias before your study begins.
  • Probability sampling: every subject has a known, non-zero chance — this allows estimation and inference.
  • Simple random sampling: every member has an equal chance; use random number tables or software; unbiased but needs a complete frame and spreads travel over wide geography.
  • Systematic sampling: pick every k-th person from a list after a random start — convenient for OPD registration queues.
  • Stratified sampling: split the frame into layers (sex, age band, urban or rural) and sample within each — guarantees a minority group is not wiped out by chance.
  • Cluster sampling: randomly select whole clusters (villages, schools, anganwadi centres) then study everyone inside — cheapest for community surveys in dispersed rural populations, at the price of design effect and lower precision.
  • Multistage sampling stacks these: random districts, then random PHCs, then households.
  • Non-probability sampling is practical, but generalisation dies — it is hypothesis-generating only.
  • Convenience sampling: whoever walks into your OPD that month — the default of most Indian student dissertations, acceptable for pilot studies only.
  • Purposive sampling: you deliberately select information-rich cases — the backbone of qualitative work.
  • Snowball sampling: each enrolled subject recruits peers from the same hidden network — essential when studying stigmatised groups such as drug users.
  • Quota sampling: fill fixed numbers in each category for speed.
  • Consecutive sampling: every eligible patient during a defined window — the least-biased clinical option and always worth naming.
  • Sample size is not a tradition of thirty per group; it is calculated from four inputs: the expected effect size or prevalence, the acceptable margin of error d, the confidence level (usually 95%, Z = 1.96), and the power (usually 80%, Z = 0.84) against the assumed type II error.
  • Formula for a proportion or prevalence: n = Z squared times p times q, divided by d squared. With no prior estimate take p = 0.5, d = 0.05, giving 384 — the number behind most Indian prevalence surveys.
  • Formula for comparing two means: n = 2 times Z-squared times s-squared divided by effect-size squared, where the standardised difference is Cohen's d.
  • Add 10 to 20 percent for attrition, and for cluster designs multiply by the design effect.
  • Too small a study misses a true effect; too large wastes scarce resources and exposes more subjects than needed to risk — both are ethical failures, which links this question to Unit 2.
  • Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (false alarm), guarded by the significance level alpha; type II error is missing a real effect, guarded by power — one minus beta.
  • Report that you calculated sample size before, not after, data collection — a post-hoc power justification reads as an excuse. In ICMR-funded multicentric trials the statistician finalises this calculation in the protocol stage.
Sources
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics.
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
410 marks

Explain the ethical principles in practice of physiotherapy in a hospital and community.

Full answer →

Give the four ethical principles with a physiotherapy example each, then contrast hospital and community practice.

  • What earns marks: the four principles with a physiotherapy example each — plus the hospital-versus-community contrast, which is where the distinction marks come from.
  • Ethics rests on two legs: the four prima facie principles of Beauchamp and Childress, and the professional codes that convert them into rules of conduct — the World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice and, for research and community programmes in India, the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines 2017.
  • Principles give the philosophy; codes give the enforceable behaviour. Quoting both lifts the answer from a philosophy essay to a professional one.
  • Autonomy: the patient's right to decide — exercised through informed consent, truth-telling about the diagnosis, and respect for refusal. An OPD patient may decline a passive-mobilisation technique, and we document and respect it.
  • Beneficence: act for the patient's benefit — choose the exercise programme with the best evidence for that person, not the most profitable for the clinic.
  • Non-maleficence: do no harm — screen for red flags, avoid over-pressure on osteoporotic spines, and apply a risk-benefit justification for every modality.
  • Justice: fairness in distribution — equal quality of care for a ward patient and a private cubicle patient, transparent fees, and no discrimination by caste, religion, gender, HIV status or ability to pay.
  • Hospital — consent: obtain it before the first assessment and again for any change of plan, in the patient's language. Remember a signature without understanding is not consent.
  • Hospital — confidentiality: no case discussions in hospital corridors, no patient photos on personal phones, and digital records protected as the ICMR data-protection expectations require.
  • Hospital — boundaries: maintain professional boundaries — no personal relationships with patients under care.
  • Hospital — documentation: record every session honestly; the case sheet is the ethical record that protects the patient and you.
  • Hospital — scope: practise within your scope and refer onwards to an orthopaedician or a physician when red flags exceed physiotherapy.
  • Hospital — honesty: follow infection control, be truthful about fees and likely outcomes, and do not promise cures — "guaranteed pain relief in three sittings" is an ethical breach, not marketing.
  • Community — voluntariness must be real: a free camp attended by the whole village because the employer sanctioned leave is not entirely voluntary.
  • Community — cultural and religious sensitivity decides whether an exercise programme is followed: prescribing knee flexion postures where squatting is required for daily life is poor rehabilitation.
  • Community — justice dominates: reach patients who cannot reach us.
  • Community — data ethics: use ICMR 2017 standards when the programme involves data collection — ethical committee approval, anonymised records, and benefit flowing back to the community studied, not only to the researchers.
Sources
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
  • World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice.
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
510 marks

Explain the instrumentation for neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES).

Full answer →

Trace the signal from mains to patient and give the parameter settings — instrumentation needs physics, not just a parameter list.

  • What earns marks: say the words transformer, rectifier, oscillator, coupling transformer and patient isolation — the physics, not just the parameter list.
  • Add the key sentence: phase duration, not the machine's frequency label, decides which tissue depolarises. That single sentence separates the 7-mark script from the 10-mark one.
  • Principle: NMES does not excite the muscle fibre directly — it depolarises the motor axon under the cathode, and the action potential travelling to the neuromuscular junction produces contraction exactly as voluntary effort does.
  • Because it bypasses the voluntary motor drive, even a patient with upper motor neuron weakness contracts.
  • Recruitment order is reversed: electrical stimulation recruits large, fast type II axons before small type I axons — the opposite of the Henneman size principle. This is why NMES fatigues muscle faster than voluntary work.
  • Block diagram, step 1 — power supply: the mains at 230 volts AC enters a step-down transformer, is rectified to DC and smoothed by a filter to give a safe, stable low-voltage supply.
  • Step 2 — oscillator: the timing circuit, classically a 555-type timer, generates the pulse train and sets frequency, phase duration and on-off timing.
  • Step 3 — output stage: a transistorised amplifier raises current to the therapeutic level, usually through a coupling transformer that isolates the patient from the mains — the safety heart of the instrument.
  • Step 4 — patient: the current reaches the skin through electrodes placed over the motor point of the target muscle.
  • Controls to memorise: frequency 20–50 Hz; phase duration 200–400 µs; duty cycle 1:1 to 1:5; ramp-up 100–300 ms; amplitude = maximum tolerated.
  • Waveform: the waveform of choice is a symmetrical or asymmetric biphasic pulsed current — balanced charge leaves no net DC component and prevents iontophoresis-like skin irritation and burns under the electrode.
  • Frequency use: low rates 2 to 10 Hz twitch the muscle for drainage and the muscle pump; 20 to 50 Hz produce tetanic contraction for strengthening; up to 80 to 100 Hz are used for spasm inhibition, at the cost of fast fatigue.
  • Phase duration: 200 to 400 microseconds sits over the strength-duration curve's comfortable motor threshold for innervated muscle.
  • Duty cycle (the on:off ratio): 1:5 in early reconditioning and about 1:1 for strengthening; more off-time means less fatigue.
  • Ramp-up and ramp-down of 100 to 300 milliseconds let the patient tolerate higher amplitude, and amplitude is turned to the maximum tolerated, aiming for a strong, comfortable tetanic contraction.
  • Electrodes: match size to muscle bulk — larger electrodes lower current density and improve comfort; placement over the motor point lowers the threshold; prep the skin and check impedance, because broken current paths cause burns.
  • Contraindications and precautions: cardiac pacemakers and implanted devices, the carotid sinus, the pregnant uterus, active deep vein thrombosis, areas of active malignancy, and sensory loss where the patient cannot report excessive current.
  • Instrument types: Russian current (medium frequency 2500 Hz, burst-modulated at 50 bursts per second, for strengthening); functional electrical stimulation (stimulation synchronised to a task such as foot-drop walking); TENS (sensory-level sibling for pain); and stimulators for denervated muscle, which must deliver long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds — often triangular or exponential — because denervated fibre has no axon to depolarise.
Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
610 marks

Explain the various study designs in research.

Full answer →

Classify designs as observational or experimental, then describe each with its statistic and its bias controls.

  • What earns marks: for every design give one physiotherapy example and one statistic it produces — odds ratio for case-control, relative risk for cohort — and for the RCT use the phrase "randomisation plus concealment plus blinding plus intention-to-treat".
  • Designs described without their bias controls read like a menu, not an answer.
  • Classification axis one: does the investigator allocate the exposure? If not, the design is observational; if yes, it is experimental.
  • Observational splits into descriptive (case report, case series, cross-sectional survey) and analytical (case-control, cohort).
  • Experimental includes the randomised controlled trial, quasi-experiment, pre-experimental pre-post designs, and the single-case (n-of-1) experiment.
  • Axis two — timing: retrospective looks backwards from outcome; prospective looks forward from exposure.
  • Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time point; they give prevalence, not incidence, and cannot prove sequence — useful for a survey of low back pain prevalence among Bengaluru autorickshaw drivers.
  • Case-control studies start from the outcome and compare past exposure between cases and controls, yielding an odds ratio; efficient for rare outcomes like transient brachial plexopathy, but memory bias is the toll.
  • Cohort studies start from exposure and follow forward for the outcome — relative risk, temporal sequence established; the ethical design when withholding treatment is impossible, at the price of time, expense and loss to follow-up.
  • Case reports and series generate hypotheses, one patient at a time.
  • RCT is the reference standard: randomisation distributes known and unknown confounders equally between groups, concealed allocation prevents selection bias, blinding of patient, therapist and assessor prevents expectation bias, and an intention-to-treat analysis preserves the randomisation.
  • State the PICO question explicitly — population, intervention, comparison, outcome — and the design becomes obvious rather than memorised.
  • Below the RCT: quasi-experimental designs (allocation by ward or by week, when randomising individuals is impossible); pre-post single-group designs (no control, only a hypothesis); the single-case experimental design with repeated baseline phases (a clinician's method for one patient); and crossover trials, where each patient is their own control and a washout period separates phases.
  • Evidence pyramid, bottom to top: expert opinion and bench research, case reports and series, case-control studies, cohort studies, RCTs, systematic reviews. Higher means better protection against bias, not automatic truth.
  • Qualitative designs answer meaning questions: phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography — analysed by the Braun and Clarke six-phase thematic analysis (for example, why patients abandon home programmes).
  • Match the design to the question: a therapy question wants an RCT or systematic review; a prognosis question wants a cohort; a diagnostic accuracy question wants a cross-sectional comparison against a gold standard; a meaning question wants qualitative work.
Sources
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
  • Herbert R et al. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
  • Braun V, Clarke V. Using thematic analysis in psychology, 2006.
710 marks

Discuss in brief parametric and non-parametric tests.

Full answer →

Pair each parametric test with its non-parametric twin, and say how to choose between them.

  • What earns marks: write the answer as a paired table — parametric test on the left, its non-parametric twin on the right — and add one line on why you chose each, e.g. "VAS pain is ordinal, so Wilcoxon signed-rank."
  • Always state the design first, then the test — a paired test on unpaired data is a more serious error than choosing the wrong family.
  • Parametric tests assume the data follow a specific distribution — the normal (Gaussian) curve — and estimate its parameters, mean and standard deviation.
  • Four assumptions of parametric tests: normality; data measured on interval or ratio scale; homogeneity of variance across compared groups; and independence of observations.
  • Non-parametric tests make no distributional assumption — hence "distribution-free" — and work on ranks, so they tolerate ordinal scales like pain scores and skewed data like hospital stay or income.
  • Check normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test, or by eyeballing the histogram and Q-Q plot — naming an actual check is worth more than reciting the assumption.
  • One group versus a known value: one-sample t-test.
  • Two paired measurements (pain before and after ten sittings of interferential therapy): paired t-test.
  • Two independent groups (conventional exercise versus physiotherapist-supervised exercise in two OPD cohorts): unpaired (independent) t-test.
  • Three or more independent groups: one-way ANOVA, with a post-hoc test such as Tukey to find which pair differs.
  • Repeated measurements across time: repeated-measures ANOVA.
  • Relationship between two continuous variables: Pearson's correlation coefficient r.
  • Each test outputs a p-value and, in modern reporting, a confidence interval. Say: p less than 0.05 means evidence against the null, not proof of a large effect.
  • Non-parametric twins — paired setting: the sign test (direction only) and the more powerful Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
  • Two independent groups: Mann-Whitney U test.
  • Three or more groups: Kruskal-Wallis H test.
  • Repeated measures: Friedman test.
  • Correlation: Spearman's rho.
  • Categorical data: the chi-square test — goodness of fit and independence in a contingency table — with Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts fall below five.
  • Choosing: normal, interval data with comparable variances choose parametric; ordinal, ranked, skewed or outlier-heavy data choose non-parametric. Both paths must still respect independence and the pairing structure of the design.
  • If the data look nearly normal, prefer the parametric test — it is more powerful, and on mildly non-normal data the rank tests retain roughly 95 percent of that efficiency, so little is lost either way.
Sources
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics.
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
810 marks

Considerations for exercise prescription in obesity.

Full answer →

Write a real prescription — pre-participation screening, then FITT-VP with numbers, using the Asian Indian cutoffs.

  • What earns marks: the answer must read as a prescription, not an essay on obesity — four FITT letters with numbers, the Asian Indian cutoffs (BMI 25, waist 90/80), and the hypoglycaemia-with-insulin warning.
  • Candidates who write "advise exercise" without numbers cap at half marks; you are prescribing a drug called movement.
  • Define your patient: obesity is excess body fat with health risk, and for Asian Indians the thresholds arrive early.
  • Asian Indian cutoffs (Misra et al. JAPI 2009): obesity is a body mass index of 25 or more (overweight 23 to 24.9) — not the Western cutoff of 30; central obesity is a waist circumference of 90 cm or more in men and 80 cm or more in women.
  • Indians develop the "thin-fat" phenotype — metabolic risk at lower BMI — which is why we screen and treat earlier.
  • Before the first session, review comorbidities: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, and painful knees or low back from the mechanical load.
  • Diabetes caution: exercise after an insulin or sulfonylurea dose risks hypoglycaemia — advise carrying glucose and adjusting the dose with the physician.
  • Blood pressure: record resting blood pressure; defer if 180/110 or above until controlled.
  • Stratify cardiovascular risk: the apparently healthy obese adult can begin moderate activity without testing, while symptomatic patients or those planning vigorous exercise need medical clearance.
  • Baseline measures to document: waist circumference, resting heart rate and blood pressure, a six-minute walk test, and functional joint status.
  • Frequency: aerobic exercise on five days a week (or every day if lighter); resistance training on two to three non-consecutive days.
  • Intensity: moderate — 40 to 60 percent of heart-rate reserve, or a talk-test pace where the patient can still converse, rating of perceived exertion 11 to 13 on the Borg 6-to-20 scale.
  • Time: 30 to 60 minutes daily, accumulated in bouts of at least ten minutes, building to the guideline volume of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity weekly.
  • Type: load-friendly aerobic choices first — brisk walking, stationary cycling, swimming or aqua exercise (buoyancy unloads the knees) — later progressing to jogging; plus large-muscle resistance training, because each kilogram of added muscle raises resting metabolic rate and preserves lean mass during weight loss.
  • Quantify energy cost in METs — brisk walking is about 4, cycling about 8 — so the patient can see that walking thirty minutes burns roughly the calories of one chapati. Diet must change in parallel: exercise alone rarely outpaces a calorie surplus.
  • Progress volume first, intensity later — add roughly five to ten minutes per fortnight of tolerated walking before touching speed or incline.
  • Protect joints: aquatic exercise, cycles and graded walking paths for the painful knee; cushioned footwear on hard Indian roads; avoid deep squats early.
  • Safety: time outdoor sessions for early morning or evening in Indian heat and humidity, and enforce hydration.
  • Behaviour and adherence: written goals, step counters, exercise logs, walking groups for company, and family involvement — in Indian households the kitchen decides the calorie side of the equation, so involve whoever cooks.
  • Reassess monthly with waist circumference and walk time, not the weighing scale alone, and coordinate with a dietitian and physician: exercise preserves lean mass during weight loss, which dieting alone squanders.
Sources
  • Misra A et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. JAPI, 2009.
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
910 marks

Differentiate aerobic and anaerobic exercise in terms of energy expenditure.

Full answer →

Contrast the two in terms of energy expenditure — which substrate, how much ATP, how fast it arrives, and the oxygen and lactate cost.

  • What earns marks: the mark is for "in terms of energy expenditure", so anchor every difference in ATP — which substrate, how much ATP per glucose molecule (2 versus about 32), how fast it arrives, and what it costs in oxygen and lactate.
  • A pure list of "aerobic means jogging" scores half; the mechanism scores full.
  • All exercise is powered by ATP, regenerated by three systems on a time-and-intensity clock.
  • Phosphagen system (stored ATP and creatine phosphate): fuels the first eight to ten seconds of all-out effort anaerobically, without oxygen, without lactate.
  • Anaerobic glycolysis: breaks glucose to pyruvate and, when oxygen supply lags demand, ferments it to lactate, regenerating ATP rapidly for roughly ten seconds to two minutes of heavy work — at the cost of hydrogen-ion accumulation and early fatigue.
  • Oxidative (aerobic) system: burns carbohydrate and fat in the mitochondria with oxygen, yielding far more ATP per glucose molecule but only at a slower rate; it dominates from about two minutes onward and supports hours of submaximal work.
  • The systems never switch on and off; they share the load, and the intensity of the exercise decides the share.
  • Intensity: aerobic work is moderate, sustainable and below the lactate threshold (roughly 55 to 70 percent of maximal oxygen uptake); anaerobic work is near-maximal, above the lactate threshold, where blood lactate climbs past about 4 mmol per litre.
  • Oxygen demand: aerobic exercise is steady state — uptake meets demand; anaerobic exercise creates an oxygen deficit that must be repaid.
  • Fuel: aerobic uses both carbohydrate and fat (fat burns only in a carbohydrate flame, and only aerobically); anaerobic burns carbohydrate alone.
  • Duration and power: anaerobic delivers high power for seconds to about two minutes; aerobic delivers lower power for minutes to hours.
  • By-products: anaerobic accumulates lactate and hydrogen ions; aerobic yields carbon dioxide and water.
  • ATP yield: anaerobic gives 2 ATP per glucose molecule versus roughly 32 aerobically.
  • Physiotherapy examples a therapist meets daily: a patient rising from a chair once (phosphagen), a stair-climbing test (glycolytic), a six-minute walk test (aerobic).
  • Oxygen deficit: at exercise onset, oxidative phosphorylation lags behind demand — covered meanwhile by the phosphagen system and glycolysis.
  • EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, the modern name for oxygen debt): after stopping, oxygen uptake remains raised — it repays the phosphagen stores, clears lactate by gluconeogenesis in the liver (the Cori cycle), restores myoglobin, and funds the raised temperature and catecholamine-driven metabolism.
  • Anaerobic exercise produces a large, fast-rising EPOC; aerobic exercise, when severe and prolonged, produces a slower but longer-lasting one — the physiological basis of interval-training prescriptions for cardiometabolic patients.
  • Aerobic training adaptations: more mitochondria and aerobic enzymes, higher capillary density and haemoglobin mass, lower resting heart rate and higher maximal oxygen uptake — tested by graded exercise tests with gas analysis or field tests like the six-minute walk or 20-m shuttle.
  • Anaerobic training adaptations: larger phosphagen stores and glycolytic enzymes, and better hydrogen-ion buffering — tested by the 30-second Wingate anaerobic test or vertical jumps.
  • For our patients, most rehabilitation is aerobic; anaerobic dosing belongs to return-to-sport phases, and the physiotherapist's skill is prescribing on the correct side of the lactate threshold.

Aerobic vs anaerobic in three numbers: 10 seconds : 2 minutes : unlimited — then name the fuel each system burns.

Sources
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
1010 marks

Describe electrical stimulation and its effect on various systems.

Full answer →

Describe the current, then its effects system by system with a mechanism for each.

  • What earns marks: the question says "various systems", so an answer that only discusses muscle caps itself at five marks — give one heading each for muscle, nerve, circulation and at least two other systems, each with a mechanism, not just a claim.
  • The type-II recruitment reversal and the pain-gate mechanism are the two most-tested mechanisms in this unit.
  • Definition: therapeutic electrical stimulation is the application of controlled electrical current through surface electrodes to excite nerve or muscle and produce a physiological or therapeutic effect.
  • Classification by pulse shape: rectangular, triangular, exponential, sinusoidal.
  • Classification by continuity: direct versus pulsed.
  • Classification by clinical intent: NMES for muscle activation, functional electrical stimulation synchronised to a task, TENS for sensory analgesia, and Russian current for strengthening.
  • Unifying mechanism: depolarisation of the excitable membrane under the cathode when the stimulus crosses the threshold defined by the strength-duration curve.
  • Muscle — contraction follows frequency: twitches below about 10 to 15 Hz, tetanic contraction from 20 to 50 Hz, and rapid fatigue above that.
  • Muscle — recruitment is reversed compared with voluntary effort: large type II motor axons fire first, which makes NMES a useful fast-twitch trainer but an early fatiguer.
  • Muscle — used repeatedly, it maintains muscle mass in disuse and immobilisation, retards atrophy after injury or surgery, strengthens weak quadriceps and pelvic floor, re-educates a muscle the patient has "forgotten" to recruit, and pumps venous and lymphatic return through the muscle pump.
  • Denervated muscle needs a different instrument entirely: long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds and triangular or exponential waveforms, because there is no axon to depolarise and the fibre itself must be excited.
  • Nervous system — sensory: low-intensity high-rate stimulation recruits large-diameter afferents and closes the pain gate in the dorsal horn (the mechanism of conventional TENS); low-rate (2 to 4 Hz) stimulation recruits descending opioid pathways for diffuse analgesia.
  • Nervous system — sensory: stimulated sensory input also improves proprioceptive awareness of a joint.
  • Nervous system — motor: stimulation preserves axonal excitability and conduction in disuse, and cyclic stimulation of the common peroneal nerve in foot drop is the classic functional application of motor-nerve stimulation.
  • Circulation: rhythmically stimulated skeletal muscle acts as a peripheral heart — the pumping action drives venous and lymphatic return, reduces oedema after injury and encourages arterial inflow.
  • Circulation: large-muscle stimulation raises heart rate and blood pressure because the metabolic demand of contracting muscle triggers sympathetic cardiovascular responses — a consideration in cardiac patients.
  • Metabolism: local metabolism rises in the stimulated muscle with increased substrate use, and stimulation-induced movement aids nutrition of cartilage and soft tissue in immobilised joints.
  • Bone: mechanical strain generates piezoelectric currents, and clinically applied electrical stimulation is used to support delayed-union fracture healing.
  • Skin and viscera: long-standing sensory stimulation can produce trophic changes; smooth muscle and viscera respond poorly to brief pulses, though some bladder and pelvic-floor applications exist.
