Q8. Describe electrical stimulation and its effect on various systems.

Full answer →

Examiners want a definition, the common types, the parameters, and a clear account of the effects on each body system, plus cautions.

  • Electrical stimulation uses controlled current to produce therapeutic effects.
  • It works because nerve and muscle membranes are electrically excitable.
  • A pulse depolarises the membrane; reaching threshold fires an action potential.
  • Types include NMES, FES, TENS, interferential therapy, high-voltage pulsed galvanic stimulation and iontophoresis.
  • Key parameters: waveform, pulse duration, frequency, intensity, duty cycle and treatment time.
  • Neuromuscular effect: produces contraction, strengthens muscle and helps re-educate movement.
  • Pain effect: activates large afferents to close the pain gate and releases natural opioids.
  • Circulatory effect: improves blood flow, venous return and reduces oedema.
  • Musculoskeletal effect: preserves muscle mass and supports tendon and bone healing.
  • Skin and wound effect: promotes healing and reduces oedema.
  • Central effect: afferent input can promote cortical plasticity after stroke or spinal cord injury.
  • Cautions: avoid over the heart, pacemakers, pregnancy, bleeding areas and where sensation is impaired.

Electrical stimulation drives nerves with current — depolarising motor axons to contract muscle and sensory axons to gate pain.

Sources
  • Prentice WE. Therapeutic Modalities in Rehabilitation. 5th ed. 2017.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. 8th ed. 2023.
  • Peng L, et al. NMES after total knee arthroplasty. Front Med. 2021;8:779019.
  • Happ KA, Behringer M. NMES vs conventional strength training. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36:3527–3540.

Q9. Write note on Muscle Plasticity in response to electrical stimulation.

Full answer →

Examiners want a definition of muscle plasticity, the neural, muscular, metabolic and functional adaptations to electrical stimulation, and a comparison with voluntary training.

  • Muscle plasticity is the muscle's ability to adapt its structure and function to activity, load or neural input.
  • Electrical stimulation provides an artificial, non-voluntary activation of muscle.
  • Electrically evoked contractions recruit motor units non-selectively and synchronously, causing rapid fatigue.
  • Neural adaptations: increased cortical and spinal excitability, BDNF upregulation and axonal sprouting.
  • Muscular adaptations: increased protein synthesis, hypertrophy, greater cross-sectional area and changes in muscle architecture.
  • Fibre-type changes occur, with increased type II fibre size in ageing muscle.
  • Metabolic adaptations: more oxidative enzymes, more mitochondria and better capillarisation.
  • Functional adaptations: gains in strength, power, endurance and preserved muscle mass.
  • It is useful when voluntary contraction is limited by pain, immobilisation or nerve injury.
  • Its effect depends on stimulation parameters, duration and the state of the nerve and muscle.
  • Effects are enhanced when combined with voluntary effort, imagery or blood-flow restriction.
  • Used after surgery, in stroke and spinal cord injury, and to counter sarcopenia.

Plasticity means the muscle rebuilds itself to match the demand — ES is an artificial demand that still remodels muscle and nerve.

Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. 2021.
  • Lieber RL. Skeletal Muscle Structure, Function, and Plasticity. 3rd ed. 2010.
  • Mettler JA, et al. Molecular and neural adaptations to NMES. J Physiol. 2021;599:2375–2399.
  • Mukherjee S, et al. Electrical stimulation and muscle strength gains. J Strength Cond Res. 2023;37:938–950.

Q10. Discuss Competency based education and compare the current education in physiotherapy.

Full answer →

Examiners want a definition of competency-based education, its key features, and a clear comparison with the traditional model, including the Indian context.

  • Competency-based education (CBE) advances a learner only when a defined competency is demonstrated.
  • A competency combines knowledge, skills and attitudes needed for real practice.
  • CBE is built on domains of competence, competencies, milestones and Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs).
  • It uses constructive alignment — outcomes, teaching and assessment matched together.
  • Teaching is learner-centred and assessment is continuous, formative and workplace-based.
  • Progression is by competence, not by time served.
  • Domains include practice, professionalism, communication, learning and development, management and research.
  • Traditional education is teacher-centred, content-driven and assessed by summative exams.
  • Traditional education often has a theory-practice gap; CBE is built around real practice tasks.
  • In India, the NCAHP Act, 2021 and the National Physiotherapy Curriculum Handbook have adopted a competency-based approach.
  • Challenges include faculty training, valid assessment tools, clinical placement quality and resource intensity.
  • Benefits include better alignment to practice, clearer expectations, accountability and patient safety.

Traditional education asks what was taught; competency-based education asks what the learner can actually do — and only then advances them.

Sources
  • WHO. Rehabilitation Competency Framework. 2020.
  • NCAHP. National Physiotherapy Curriculum Handbook. 2023.
  • Fitzpatrick JA, et al. Fundamentals of competency-based education in physical therapy. J Phys Ther Educ. 2024;38(2):1.
  • Frank JR, et al. Competency-based medical education: theory to practice. Med Teach. 2010;32:638–645.

Glossary of difficult terms (76)

Dotted-underlined words also show the definition on hover or tap.

  • allodynia — Pain from a stimulus that is not normally painful.
  • arthrogenic muscle inhibition — Reflex weakness of a muscle caused by a problem inside its joint (abbreviated AMI).
  • arthrokinematics — The small gliding, rolling and spinning movements between joint surfaces.
  • atrophy — Wasting or shrinking of muscle or tissue.
  • biomechanics — The study of the mechanical laws relating to the movement of living organisms.
  • biopsychosocial — An approach that considers biological, psychological and social factors together.
  • capsular pattern — The characteristic order in which a joint loses range when the whole capsule is involved.
  • capsule — The fibrous sleeve that surrounds and stabilises a joint.
  • catastrophising — Interpreting pain in an exaggerated, worst-case way.
  • central sensitisation — Increased excitability of the central nervous system that makes normal inputs feel painful.
  • collagen — The main structural protein in tendon, ligament, skin and bone.
  • concentric — Muscle work while it shortens under load (the lifting phase).
  • contracture — A permanent tightening or shortening of tissue that restricts movement.
  • contraindication — A condition that makes a treatment unsafe or inadvisable.
  • creep — Slow progressive lengthening of tissue under a constant sustained load over time.
  • cryotherapy — Treatment using cold.
  • dermatome — The area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • dorsal horn — The rear part of the spinal cord's grey matter where sensory nerves first relay pain signals.
  • dorsiflexion — Bending the ankle or wrist so the angle at the front decreases (e.g. lifting the toes up).
  • eccentric — Muscle work while it lengthens under load (the lowering phase).
  • effleurage — A smooth gliding massage stroke.
  • effusion — Fluid collecting inside a joint.
  • electrotherapy — Treatment using electrical currents or electromagnetic energy.
  • end-feel — The quality of resistance felt at the very end of a joint's movement, used to judge what limits it.
  • eversion — Turning the sole of the foot outward.
  • fear-avoidance — Avoiding activity because of fear of pain, which over time worsens disability.
  • gait — The manner of walking.
  • gate control theory — The idea that non-painful input (rubbing, TENS) can 'close a gate' in the spinal cord and reduce pain.
  • golgi tendon organ — A sensor in tendon that detects tension and helps regulate muscle force.
  • goniometry — Measuring joint angles with a goniometer.
  • hyperalgesia — An increased sensitivity to pain.
  • hypermobility — Excessive movement at a joint, usually from lax or torn ligaments.
  • hypertrophy — An increase in muscle or tissue size.
  • hypomobility — Reduced movement at a joint, usually from tight or stiff tissue.
  • ICF — The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health.
  • inflammation — The body's protective response to injury - heat, redness, swelling and pain.
  • inversion — Turning the sole of the foot inward.
  • isometric — A muscle contraction with no change in length (no joint movement).
  • joint play — The small accessory movement available at a joint beyond voluntary control.
  • kinesiophobia — Fear of movement or of re-injury.
  • laser therapy — Red/near-infrared light therapy that stimulates cell repair (photobiomodulation).
  • ligament — Strong fibrous tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises a joint.
  • manipulation — A quick, small thrust applied to a joint by a clinician.
  • manual muscle testing — Grading a muscle's strength by resisting a voluntary contraction (abbreviated MMT).
  • mechanoreceptors — Sensory receptors that detect mechanical stimuli such as touch, pressure and joint position.
  • mechanotransduction — How cells turn mechanical load into chemical signals that change the tissue.
  • moment arm — The perpendicular distance from a force to the joint axis; a longer moment arm produces more torque.
  • muscle spindle — A stretch sensor inside muscle that helps control posture and movement.
  • myofascial — Relating to muscle and its surrounding fascia.
  • myotome — The group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • neurodynamic — Relating to the mechanical and physiological function of nerves; neural mobilisation treats nerve sensitivity.
  • nociceptive — Relating to the detection of painful stimuli.
  • nociceptor — A sensory nerve ending that detects painful or tissue-damaging stimuli.
  • oedema — Swelling caused by fluid trapped in the tissues.
  • osteokinematics — The visible movements of bones at a joint, such as flexion and extension.
  • outcome measure — A standardised tool used to measure a patient's status or change over time.
  • palpation — Examining the body by touch to feel for tenderness, swelling or tissue change.
  • plantarflexion — Pointing the foot downward, as when standing on tiptoe.
  • posture — The position of the body and its parts relative to gravity.
  • precaution — A situation requiring extra care during treatment.
  • proprioception — The sense of body and joint position and movement.
  • proprioceptive — Relating to the body's sense of position and movement.
  • radiculopathy — A nerve-root problem causing pain, numbness or weakness along a limb.
  • range of motion — How far a joint can move (abbreviated ROM).
  • red flag — A sign or symptom suggesting serious pathology that needs medical referral.
  • ROM — Short for range of motion - how far a joint can move.
  • sensitivity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who have the condition.
  • special test — A clinical test used to confirm or rule out a specific structure or condition.
  • specificity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have the condition.
  • synovial — Relating to the fluid-filled lining of a joint.
  • tendinopathy — A tendon disorder causing pain and reduced function.
  • tendon — Strong fibrous tissue that attaches muscle to bone.
  • TENS — Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation - a mild current passed through the skin to relieve pain.
  • torque — A turning force around an axis - the product of force and its moment arm.
  • traction — A gentle pulling force applied to a joint or the spine to relieve pressure.
  • trigger point — A tender, tight knot in a muscle that can refer pain elsewhere.
